Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As mentioned a a few days ago, a draft Order in Council has been prepared containing an amended scale of pensions. It is not necessary that there should be any legislation making these effective, because, so far as troops in Canada are concerned, pensions are fixed under the provisions of the Pension Act and the scale can be altered from time to time. The Minister of Justice has advised us that the scale of pensions proposed with regard to troops serving in Canada can he applied under the War Measures Act to troops serving overseas. It is, however, desirable that the House should be made acquainted with what we propose, and that an opportunity should be given for discussion, if desired; therefore, I wish to lay upon the table of the House a copy of the proposed Order in Council. It has not yet been passed, and will not be passed until the House has an opportunity of making suggestions and expressing an opinion upon it. It is in the final form which we propose, with the possible exception of a minor modification which has been suggested to me within the past day or two by the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, and which I have not yet had an opportunity of considering. I 
will send a couple of copies across to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in order that he may make whatever suggestions he may desire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAKE OF THE WOODS TECHNICAL BOARD.
speechtext:
I should like to give the House some information which, in reply to an inquiry made a day or two ago either by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition or by the hon. member for St. John, I promised to bring down with regard to the work which is being done in regard to the Lake of the Woods.
The Lake of the Woods Technical Board was formed by Order in Council on the 2nd of March, 1914. It consists of five permanent officers of the various departments: Mr. Chapleau, representing the Department of Public Works; Mr. Fraser, representing the Department of Marine and Fisheries; Mr. Challies, representing the Department of the Interior; Mr. Stewart, representing the Department of Naval Service; and Mr. Acres, representing the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission. The work assigned to it is a study of conditions on and around the Lake of the Woods both before any artificial works were placed in the watershed and since, with a view to advising the Government as to the best course to pursue in the interests of Canada itself. For this purpose it is necessary to gather all the available information from dominion, provincial and private records, relating principally to the water levels, to ascertain what may be called high water, what may be called low water, and what may be called mean water. So far as possible, records for discharges and supply must be carefully examined so that the board may know what is the available supply of water, and what quantity may reasonably be expected for power purposes. When the hoard has sifted these records and the information, it will be expected definitely to fix the range within which the level of the various lakes of the watershed will be controlled, and of course advise as to whether the conservation of all the water will necessitate the flooding of any of the shores, and, if so, to what extent.
So far, the board has had the services of only one engineer and an assistant gathering this data. It has fortunately been able to avail itself of old records and surveys made by various departments. The gauge records, which are of course of the utmost importance, have not been very well kept in the past, and their co-relation has necessitated a great

deal of labour, but it is hoped that during the coming year everything will be straightened out.
This information has been furnished me in the shape of a memorandum by Mr. William J. Stewart, who is a member of the commission, and who is acting in a special capacity, as has been explained to the House, with the purpose of assisting the Government in connection with matters that come under the consideration of the International Joint Commission.

1.	That it is expedient to provide that a sum not exceeding one hundred million dollars ($100,000,000) be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred by or under the authority of the Governor in Council during the year ending the 31st day of March, 1916, for:

speechtext: Yes. I have asked the various departments to make a memorandum for me of all information that we could foresee as likely to be called for. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: I suppose it would be quite agreeable if, on the naval and militia estimates, one were to make suggestions as to the method of expenditure, or departmental policy as to details, and to discuss it upon that occasion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would be very glad indeed to have some suggestions from my hon. friends on the other side of the House. As fari as this vote is concerned, we regard it as not a vote for any particular department of the Government, and therefore as a vote as to which the Governor in Council has a special and important responsibility. Consequently the expenditures under it have been required to be authorized by Order in Council. That principle was necessarily departed from in the first two or three weeks of the war, because expenditures which were properly chargeable to this vote had been made before the vote was actually passed by Parliament. These expenditures were made principally by the Department of Militia and Defence, and the course taken was this. The department made a complete report of these expenditures, with, I think, all the important vouchers. That was presented to Council and was referred by Council to the Treasury Board, which made a pretty careful investigation into it as far as they were able to. do so. Then, the report of the Treasury Board in regard to these expenditures was submitted to Council, and, if my memory serves me correctly, was ratified by Council. It was then provided by Order in Council, which I think was laid on the table of the House, that no expenditures under ! this appropriation should be made except under the authority of Council. That course has been acted upon since. I am obliged to my right hon. friend for his suggestions as to the information which is desired, and I must say that his request in that regard is entirely reasonable. I will ask the several ministers, who have had anything to do with the matters which he has mentioned, to be prepared with the necessary information when the House is in committee on the Bill.

As far as the defence and security of Canada are concerned, I might say one word at the present moment. In connection with the military defence of the country, of course there are many matters that are of a confidential character; but I should be very glad indeed, with respect to these confidential matters, to communicate any facts of importance to my right hon. friend or to any of the members on the other side of the House who might desire to be made especially acquainted with them. One subject Ithat necessarily engaged our attention in the early part of the war was the security of public buildings and structures belonging -to the people of Canada and under the control of the Government. The course which we took in that regard was this: An Order in Council was passed directing that any department of the Government which might think it necessary to have military protection for the buildings or works or structures in question, should communicate with the Department of Militia and Defence, and the department was instructed to provide, and undertook the responsibility of providing, any military protection which might be necessary. As far as other buildings, works or structures were concerned, it might happen that the department would feel that police protection would be more advisable than military protection. The same Order in Council provided that if such was the opinion of any department of the Government, then the minister, or the officers of that department, should communicate with the Minister of Justice, and the commissioner of Dominion Police was given all necessary power and authority to add immediately to the police force under his charge as might be necessary for carrying out the requirements of any department of the Government.
In regard to " the continuance of trade, industry and business communications," my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has had a great deal of work and a great deal of responsibility in that regard, as to which he will be prepared, either now or when the House is in committee on the Bill, to give full information to the House and to the country.
If any hon. gentleman on either side of the House should suggest that there is any information which it may be desirable to afford when the House is in Committee on the Bill, I shall be glad to have him mention it now or to send me a memorandum, and the Government will of course deem it
its duty to afford all such information, so far as it is not of a confidential character.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.

speechtext: On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 79, to authorize certain extensions of time to insurance companies, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Does this apply to all insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only modification
made by this Bill is that it provides a method whereby a company that has not yet taken out its license, and which may be in a position where it expects to be able ' to do so before the next session may, upon payment of one hundred dollars, obtain an extension until next session from the Superintendent of Insurance. The reason for this Bill is that it was anticipated that present conditions might bring about applications for a large number of extensions by special Bill for each company, and it was thought desirable to avoid that by making a general provision in this Bill.

I wish to bring to the
attention of the Minister of Finance a matter which is disturbing many of our business men in eastern Nova Scotia, and it is that the fire insurance underwriters in that province have given notice of their intention to increase the premiums by 30 per cent. I understand that there is no machinery under our law by which the Government can interfere, and that it has been the policy of all Governments to allow fire insurance companies a free hand in this matter, the reason being that there are numerous fire insurance companies in this country, and that they will in the ordinary course of business not unduly increase their premiums because of the competition. The fact is that in the various provinces insurance is controlled entirely by three or four men, and in that way any competition which there might be between the companies is avoided. I was speaking a day or two ago to the Superintendent of Insurance, who is a very cordial

gentleman, and who, I believe, understands his business thoroughly, and he tells me that fire insurance companies in the Maritime Provinces are losing money. It is a very serious thing for the business men in eastern Nova Scotian towns, Glaca Bay, Sydney, and I think every town with the possible exception of Pictou, that they should be called upon to pay what I consider exorbitant fire insurance premiums. If the premiums received by these companies up to the present have enabled them to carry on business with a fair margin of profit, I think there should be some machinery brought into force by which they should be prohibited from attempting to raise the premiums to such an enormous extent as 30 per cent. I fear that very many business men will in consequence be unable to obtain the privilege of insuring their buildings and property. I suppose it really comes under the Department of Finance, but I would ask the Minister of Justice if there is no way by which these fire insurance companies, when they make application for renewal of their licenses, cannot have it brought forcibly to their attention that they should conduct their affairs on ordinary business principles, and that they are not to be permitted to increase the premiums so enormously. I would impress on the Finance Department the necessity of taking control over fire insurance companies, in so far as their premium rates are concerned. I have been receiving six or seven letters every day from towns in my constituency, containing protests against the insurance companies, and the people believe that there is power in the Department of Finance to control and regulate these premiums. I think it would be a good thing if the Government would take such power at the very first opportunity. Fire insurance companies are institutions which are absolutely necessary in the business life of the community, and when we give them extensive privileges to do business they should not be allowed to do anything like charging exorbitant insurance premiums. There is not the great necessity for persons carrying life insurance as there is for business men carrying fire insurance, and consequently the life insurance companies and fire insurance com-paies are not in the same position, but in my view there certainly should be some control over the fire insurance companies.
I am taking this opportunity of bringing this matter to the attention of the Government, because perhaps an opportunity may not arise again. The Superintendent of Insurance told me that he would send me 
a statement showing the business standing of the insurance companies in the Maritime Provinces; and when I get that, I would like to submit it to the Minister of Justice for his perusal. If he thinks they are going beyond what is a fair business proposition in raising those rates, the department should take the matter into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The present Bill merely provides a method of extending the time for the taking out of licenses by companies which have not already taken them out. I am not aware of anything that can be described as a combine amongst the companies to raise rates unduly. If there were, it might be possible for some action to be taken. Furthermore, so far as my information goes, I do not believe that fire insurance companies are making a great deal of money out of their business at the present rates. Should, however, the hon. member obtain,the information that he hopes to obtain, and communicate it to me, as he suggests, I shall be very glad to look into it and consider whether there is any possible action that would be called for and justified in our department.

On motion of Hon. W.. T. White (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 75, to amend the Customs Tariff, 1907, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-Short title:

Before we take into consideration the different sections, I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the question of the duty upon fertilizers. I was very much pleased at the Minister exempting fertilizers from the increase in the duty and restoring nitrates to the free list and also putting some of the ingredients of fertilizers upon the free list; but I would respectfully urge upon him the desirability of putting manufactured fertilizers upon the free list, that is, of going a little further than he has gone. It would be in the interest of the country if that were done. A very earnest and energetic campaign is being made by the officials of the Department of Agriculture in regard tc increased production. In view of the necessities of the country and of the Empire so far as foodstuffs are concerned, even householders

who haye opportunities for gardening are urged to go into the raising of vegetables.
I noticed within a day or two an advertisement issued by the Department of Agriculture urging those who have hack yards even to utilize them as vegetable gardens. Such work cannot be done with any degree of success except by the use of fertilizers. The duty is not very large-only some $60,000; but it is paid very largely by the farmers in the Maritime Provinces. I do not think that, in proportion to the population, fertilizers are used to the same extent in Ontario as in the Maritime Provinces. In the West they are hardly used at all; but to the farmers and gardeners in the Maritime Provinces the question is a most serious one. The duty at present amounts to something over $2 per ton. That is quite a burden upon the farmers. At this time, when such an effort is being made on the part of the Department of Agriculture to stimulate the farmers to increased production, it is desirable to grant this request. I have been urged by those who take an interest in the subject to bring the matter again to the attention of the Government.
I do it in the hope that it is not too late to consider the matter favourably. I am informed-and I have no doubt that it is the case-that this is the only country in the world which imposes a duty upon fertilizers.. In the Commonwealth of Australia, not only has the Government made fertilizers free, but the Government railways carry fertilizers to the' farmers absolutely free of any charge whatever. In view of that, this Government might very well act upon my suggestion and place fertilizers upon the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the Government has exempted from the operation of the war tax both unmanufactured and manufactured fertilizers. Under item 662, unmanufactured fertilizers, including phosphate rock, German potash salts and German mineral potash, bone-dust, charred bone and bone ash, fish offal or refuse and animal or vegetable manures, are left as they were upon t!he free list. Under item 663, fertilizers compounded or manufactured, n.o.p., were formerly subject to a duty of 10 per cent general and 5 per cent British preferential. I think that item is left as it was.
My remarks are based upon that item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore, the former
tariff is in effect so far as manufactured and
unmanufactured fertilizers are concerned. The Government also, as my hon. friend has observed, has exempted from the operation of the war tariff rate acid phosphate of lime, sulphate of ammonia, nitrate of soda, muriate and sulphate of potash, imported to be used for fertilizing purposes. With regard to the latter item, some of these articles are manufactured in Canada. The duty upon the compounded. fertilizers of 10 per cent general and 5 per cent British preferential is a very small duty. It has been in the tariff for some time. My hon. friend,
I hope, has not overlooked the fact that there are a number of establishments in Canada engaged in the manufacture of fertilizers. By reason of the war taxation that we are imposing, the cost of manufacturing these goods is increased. If the duty was not unfair to the consumer before, and as we have increased the cost to the manufacturer of fertilizers in Canada, our allowing the tax to remain as it was is certainly not unfair to the consumer. The Canadian manufacturer has to compete with the American manufacturer in the Canadian market. The amount of duty is not large. I am satisfied that the farmers would not have complained, having regard to the object . of this extra taxation-to provide revenue for war purposes or for the purposes of Government in time of war and due to the exigencies of the war-had we allowed the proposals to stand as they were. But, having regard to the fact that the Department of Agriculture was carrying on this propaganda which has been referred to by my hon. friend, and that it had been drawn to our attention in connection with that propaganda that it might facilitate the work of the department and increase production this year, we are glad to take the action which I have described and exempt from the war tariff rate the fertilizers, manufactured and unmanufactured, that I have mentioned. Giving the matter the best consideration of which I am capable, I think our action will not be complained of by the agricultural community, but that,' on the contrary, they will approve of what we have done. My hon. friend will not overlook the fact, I am sure, that there are in Canada numerous establishments engaged in the manufacture of fertilizers and employing a great number of men. It will be hardly fair to diminish the very small rate of duty at present existing under the tariff of 1907, especially in view of the fact that we are increasing the cost to these manufacturers

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: of their coal, their machinery and other things used in connection with their enterprise.

I do not know that mv argument would raise the question whether the farmers would complain or not. That is not my point; my point is that agricultural production should be stimulated by this Government. We cannot stimulate production merely by advertising in the newspapers. If we wish the farmers to produce more, the way to stimulate their production is to assist them and to cheapen the cost of implements and the other things they have to use, including fertilizers.
12 noon. I believe that the Government will spend in this campaign for increased production a larger sum of money in preaching to the farmers than the whole duty on fertilizers will amount to. You can stimulate production much better by putting fertilizers on the free list. My bon. friend speaks of the manufacture of fertilizers in Canada. I do not believe that the principle of protection should be considered at all in the question of plant food, that which gives life and growth to plants, and fertilizers are essentially plant food. I believe they should be absolutely free from duty, and the farmer should be permitted to purchase fertilizers wnerever he can get them and at the lowest possible cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Fertilizers were plant food in 1907, and in the years up to 1911, just as much as they are plant food to-day. But the hon. gentleman seems now to have suddenly reached the conclusion that fertilizers are plant food and should be entirely exempt from custom duties. He says he has not called attention to this matter by reason of any consideration of whether the farmers will complain or not. It is perfectly obvious to me why he has called attention to it. I thought we had concluded the political discussion of these tariff duties on the second reading of the Bill. But if the hon. gentleman wishes to discuss the question of what this Government has done for the farmers compared with what the former Government did, I will be ready to go into that now or at any other time.
I confess it does not seem to me particularly desirable to do so. The Budget I have brought down is a budget eminently favourable to the farming community. The hon. gentleman is aware that this Government last year reduced the duty on harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers 
from 17) per cent to 12) per cent. In explaining to the House that we have exempted these items from the war tariff rate, I explained also that we were ready to do it because of the drawback to the manufacturers of these implements upon the amount of duty paid in respect of raw material entering into the production. The tariff proposals which we have brought down also exempts binder twine. I have pointed out that fertilizers, manufactured and unmanufactured, have been left precisely as they were-in other words, they have been exempted from the operation of the war taxation. I should also mention the exempting of ditching machines. I may say in a word that the tariff proposals are made having regard to the promotion of agriculture, which this Government has always had very much at heart. If my hon. friend has any doubt as to that, I would suggest that he look at the Estimates of expenditure on agriculture under this Government, as contrasted with their predecessor. Nor will he fail to bear in mind the ten million dollar Agricultural Bill introduced and carried into legislation by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell). I do not agree with my hon. friend from St. John City that nothing can be done by urging increased production. I am of the opinion that a great deal can be done by urging increased production, on the ground that at this juncture of the Empire's affairs it is a patriotic duty as well as an economical advantage to increase production. I think there has been a splendid response to the appeal made by the Department of Agriculture and the Government for increased production in Canada during this year; and I shall be very much surprised if results are not exceptionally striking when the returns of this harvest come in: The Department of Agriculture will continue its propaganda, and, as I say, I think its effects will be very striking. So far as the tariff proposals are concerned, I am anxious to avoid, if possible, the discussion of political questions in committee, but if my hon. friend desires that the issue shall be discussed now, I am prepared to discuss it, as I was prepared to discuss it when the resolutions were under debate in the House.

I raised no political
question; I simply raised my voice on behalf of increased production in this country, yet I am met with an intimation from my hon. friend that if we attempt to make any suggestions to the Government as to improving the condition of the farmers and

relieving them from the burden which the tariff imposes upon them, we will be charged with discussing political questions and my hon. friends be tempted to enter into a long disquisition as to what the Government has been doing for agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has a perfect right to raise any question he desires; I am not challenging his right to do so.

Then why does my hon. friend lecture me when I raise the question? My hon. friend says that the Government have considered this tariff and, in effect, that they have made up their minds that they will not budge one iota from the position that they have taken, no matter what suggestions may be made. My hon. friend had that same frame of mind when the Budget was brought down, but before the discussion was over he was compelled to budge from his position and to grant concessions and to make reductions and exemptions. Although I am a member of the Opposition, and in the minority, I represent a large portion of the people of Canada, and it is my duty to submit for the consideration of the Government any views which I entertain with reference to the tariff or to other matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend in that.

While I agree with the minister that the propaganda which is being carried on by the Government in favour of increased production is a good one, I wish to point out that the farmers will engage more heartily in the work of increased production-which means more machinery, the employment of more team work and of more help, and the buying of more fertilizers-if the cost of such production is reduced to the lowest possible figure. The Government are spending a larger sum of money in advertising this propaganda in the newspapers than these duties upon fertilizers will amount to; if they really want to stimulate production they will place fertilizers on the free list. My hon. friend says that fertilizers were plant food some years ago, just as they are to-day. So they were, but some years ago there was not, from the standpoint of Empire, the demand for increased production in Canada that there is to-day. It is poor policy for the Government to plead with the farmers to engage in increased production and at the same time to tax them for the plant food which is necessary to bring about
that increased production. That is the argument which I make, ana my hon. friend cannot turn the attention of this House or of the people of Canada from that question by saying thai I am introducing politics. I appeal to the minister in good faith and with the utmost earnestness that he take into consideration the advisability of doing away with this burden upon the people. At this time, when the production of foodstuffs is of enormous importance, surely it is an invidious and deplorable position for Canada to be placed in that she is to-day the only country in the world which imposes a duty upon fertilizers. I believe that every country in the world admits fertilizers absolutely free of duty, recognizing that it is in the interests not only of the farmers but of the whole country that plant food should be placed at the disposal of the farmers at the lowest possible cost.

Will duty be collected on
f.o.b. basis at point of purchase or on value established where the goods cross the frontier?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable just at the moment to quote the precise words of the Act, but duty will be collected upon the fair market value of the goods in the country of origin or at the place of exoort. If the goods were bought in New York, the duty would be imposed upon the fair market selling price of the goods in New York.

The other evening in discussing the Budget, the hon. member for Calgary said that cement can be purchased in England at GO cents a barrel and in the United States at 80 cents a barrel. Would duty be collected on cement coming into Canada on the basis of 60 cents a barrel, or would the cost of freight be added to that to establish the value for duty purposes ? During the few days that the Government were collecting duty on cotton seed meal, I had complaints from a Canadian purchaser of that commodity who had purchased cotton seed meal at $29 delivered in Montreal. Cotton seed meal had been worth $24 f.o.b. at point of shipment in the South, but owing to an advance in price, when it reached Montreal _the price was $29 delivered. The Customs Department collected duty on the basis of a ' valuation of $34. Will this method be followed when the new tariff goes into operation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government has not changed the basis upon which the new

tariff will operate; it will be subject to the provisions of the Customs Tariff of 1907, of which it is an amendment. I am unable to express an opinion upon' the particular question to which my hon. friend draws attention, for the reason that I have not all the facts before me; it is a matter of administration by the Customs Department. Referring to the question of the purchase of cement in the United States or Great Britain, the duty would be levied upon the selling price at the place where the goods were bought. If the cement were bought in England or in the United States, a customs entry would be made showing the cost price at which the cement had been bought, and subject to the dumping provisions of our legislation, duty would be imposed upon that cost. Of course the consumer would have to pay freight, but customs duty is not imposed upon freight charges.

The minister can see from
his own statement that during the few days the Customs Department were collecting duty on cotton seed meal they did not collect the duty on the basis now laid down by the minister, because this cotton seed was originally purchased at equal to $24 f.o.b. in Tennessee. In the meantime cotton seed meal advanced, it is true, and the department ruled that the fair market price of cotton seed meal in the states of Vermont and New York where it crossed the border was $34. They collected the duty on a valuation of $34, but even after that ruling the freight was $5 a ton, so that the value of that cotton seed meal should not have been placed at $34, but at not more than $299 a ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to be taken as expressing any opinion upon a particular transaction. The Commissioner of Customs is an exceedingly well-posted man, and I am quite satisfied there would be some explanation of the action taken by the Customs Department in the case referred to by my hon. friend. If he is interested in pursuing the subject, I would refer him to the Customs Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have always understood, and I know that it is so, that the duty is collected upon the selling price in the country of origin. In the case which has just been called to my hon. friend's attention, the country of origin of cotton seed meal is the United States, the place of origin being the state of Tennessee, and there the price was $24 a ton. But the 
United States is a very large country, and it may be that the Vermont price would be very different from the Tennessee price. I would imagine that under such circumstances the ruling price of the customs appraisers would be the price paid in Tennessee, not that paid in Vermont. There may be some cases that would have to be investigated, but I would imagine that it ought to be the ruling price in the place of origin that would govern for purposes of valuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think that
would lead to a great deal of difficulty and a good deal of imposition. The country of origin is what rules, not the single locality in which the article is sold to the purchaser who brings it into Canada. My hon. friend will easily see that otherwise mistakes would be apt to happen. In the first place, it would be almost impossible to have any uniformity in the tariff, so far as the imposition of duty is concerned, if you had recourse and reference to each separate locality. That would be a great deal of trouble and make the tariff almost unworkable. You might have in a single locality a set of circumstances in reference to which the ruling average selling price would be cut down on account of special circumstances, and that would scarcely be fair. My right hon. friend is exactly right, it is the country of origin that rules; and where you have different localities in a country there is some machinery by which the Customs Department gets at what is the fair average value.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Such a ruling would be very unfair in a country as large as the United States. It is impossible that an article of this character which is produced in only one locality can have the same ruling price in the north as in the south; there must be a difference, and under some circumstances it seems to me that the country of origin ought to be limited to the place where the article is grown or manufactured.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They have no doubt some general ruling in the Customs Department which they follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Here is a case in point. The hon. member for Huntingdon represents that an article which was purchased for $24 a ton in Tennessee, when it came to be appraised was appraised at $34.

That is an advance of $10. There is something there which cannot be explained here, and I would advise my bon. friend to go to the Commissioner of Customs and see what is the reason.

The matter will be made right because now the Government have notified importers that they are going to refund the duty and there will be no loss. But the United States imports large quantities of Canadian bran, and the Ontario millers practically are cut out of that business so long as the man west of the Great Lakes has bran to sell because the duty, I think, .is now 10 per cent-it used to be 20 per cent-and the bran is sold on a basis of f.o.b. Fort William and on that basis Washington rules they should collect the duty; whereas when bran would be $16 Foil William, the Montreal miller would have to sell it at $19 Montreal, so that it practically shuts out the eastern man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Section 40 of the Customs Act says:
Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof, when sold for home consumption, in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time when the same were exported directly to Canada.
What I said therefore must be taken as subject to this section of the statute, which govern the Customs Tariff, 1907, and will govern in the case of this special war taxation. We are not changing the basis upon which the taxation is levied.

That means the retail market price, I suppose.

On motion of Hon. W. T. W'hite (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 76, to supplement the revenue required to meet war expenditures, was ' read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-Short title:
Is it the practice to use the word "war" in such a Bill, or merely to designate it as a revenue Bill? I am not objecting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government's view is that this is a war revenue measure; that view has been advanced in the debate on the resolutions, and we think that this
might properly be called "The Special War Revenue Act, 1915."
Although no part of the revenue will be used for war purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Is there the same rate
on a 50-cent message as on a message costing $100?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is that fair?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I pointed out the other
day that it is not advisable that cable messages should be enhanced in cost to the public.

There is a discrimination against the poor people. Large corporations get cable messages frequently, but poor people get them very rarely. Very often a poor person will get a message announcing the death of some one or some other very important event. On the north shore of the St. Lawrence, on the Gaspe peninsula, on the Magdalen islands and in parts of British Columbia, there are Government telegraphs. I do not think the minister settled the point last night as to whether or not tolls would be exacted on messages coming over those Government lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am of the opinion that
the tolls would not be payable because by this Bill we have not made the Crown specifically liable to pay them.
The Government would require power to recover this tax from the sender of the message; otherwise it would have no authority.

Will the minister tell us
under what basis of equity he imposes an extra tax upon postage and upon telegrams and exempts telephones?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought I explained
that here the other day. No doubt my hon. friend was absent from the House on that occasion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He was present, but he was not convinced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At all events, I gave the

The minister means longdistance messages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am speaking of telephone messages generally. On section 12-stamp duties on cheques and certain other instruments:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are certain modifications which I have to suggest in this part of the Bill. So far as they relate to section 12, which covers stamp duties on cheques and certain other instruments, the following explanation may be helpful to the committee:
Stamps on cheques and other instruments had, as the Bill stood on first reading, to be affixed and cancelled by the person issuing the cheque. Such cancellation was to be effected by the party writing on or across the stamp initials or other marks of identification, together with the date of such writing. With the change the stamp will still be affixed by the party issuing the cheque, but the cancellation will not be effected until the cheque reaches the bank for payment, when by simply impressing lines across the stamp at the time of payment the bank will cancel it. We desire to avoid inconvenience to the public. I think the explanations will be readily comprehended by the committee.
Would the minister mind repeating that? The wording is somewhat obscure towards the end?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the United Kingdom, as my hon. friend knows, there is a stamp tax on cheques and promissory notes and bills of exchange. There is a provision in their legislation whereby those stamps are
to bo affixed by the party drawing the cheque or bill of exchange or promissory note; and he is required to cancel the stamp by writing across it his initials, together with the date on which it is cancelled. The legislation there, I believe, is general. Our legislation is confined to the case of cheques drawn upon banks, as defined in the Act, and promissory notes and bills of exchange negotiated through banks. In order to avoid inconvenience to the public-because it is an inconvenience for a man issuing a cheque or a promissory note or bill of exchange to write his initials across the stamp and the date on which the stamp is cancelled-it occurred to us that we would simplify matters by providing, as I have indicated here, that the party drawing the cheque or bill of exchange or promissory note should affix the stamp but that it should be cancelled by the bank paying it or negotiating it, just as the postmaster cancels a stamp upon a letter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is an improvement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore, if the committee will permit, I should like to move these amendments:
In subsection 2 of section 12, in the fourth line, after the words " of the value of two cents," strike out the remainder of the subsection and insert:
Every adhesive stamp affixed to a cheque shall be cancelled by the hank at which the cheque is payable at or before the time of payment.
The following amendment to subsection 3, line 38, after the first word, " and," strike out the remainder of the subsection, and insert:
Every adhesive stamp affixed to a bill of exchange or promissory note transferred or delivered as aforesaid shall be cancelled by the bank at the time of transfer or delivery.
In subsection 4, line 5, all after the word " and " near the end of the line is to be struck out and the following inserted :
Every adhesive stamp affixed to such receipt shall be cancelled by the bank at the time the money is paid.
In subsection 6, in the 4th line, after the word " Part," insert: " Or authorized to be used in lieu thereof/'; and in line 24, after the word " stamp," strike out:
By writing on or across the stamp initials identifying the bank, together with the date of such writing.

In subsection 7, line 30, after the words " two cents," strike out the remainder down to the words " shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars."
In subsection 8, line 45, after the words " two cents," strike out the remainder of the subsection down to the words: " Shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars."
In subsection 9, line 9, strike out the words "and over" and-the remainder of the subsection down to the words: " Shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars."
Then, strike out subsection 11 and insert:
Every bank which omits or neglects to cancel, in accordance with the requirements of this section, the adhesive stamp affixed to (a) a cheque, a bill of exchange or promissory note, (b)' a receipt for money, shall be liable to a penalty of $100.
I am sorry that all these changes are necessitated by the modification in principle which I have explained to the committee.
It is better to change them than to let them go through.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The change is certainly an improvement. It will save a lot of worry to those who have to affix the stamp, and the revenue cannot suffer from it, because a cheque cannot be paid until the stamp is erased. But I rose especially to call the attention of the minister to paragraph 4 of section 12:
" Bank " means any one receiving money he repays by honouring the cheques of the person from or on whose account the money was received.
Is it the intention of the minister that this should apply to country merchants or notaries public such as we have in the province of Quebec, who receive money on deposit, or to whom will it apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If any one acts as a banker, if he holds money on deposit for his customers subject to cheque, the Act will apply. Otherwise you would have one law applying to banks and financial institutions and another to private individuals receiving money upon deposit. That would hardly be fair. We gave the word "bank" a wide definition, so as to cover not only the chartered banks but banking institutions and private bankers receiving money upon deposit subject to cheque.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The difficulty is to know where to draw the line. I understand very well that every one who

acts as a private banker, or who receives money on deposit and who does a regular banking business, should be subject to this Act, but my hon. friend is aware that in the province of Quebec merchants and notaries are in the habit of receiving money on deposit. Is it intended that they should also be subject to this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The test of a bank, as I understand it, is that the party receiving money on deposit undertakes to pay by honoring the cheque of his customer. If a private individual receives money on deposit subject to cheque, he will be regarded as a banker. If. on the other hand, he receives money which he repays in some other way than by honoring the cheque of his customer, or if he has engaged to pay in some other way than by honouring the cheque of his customer, I would say that he would not be a banker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: 1 am afraid that will lead to some confusion.

According to the reading of the Act it appears that every man who has money in the bank on current account, and who is chequing it out in amounts of $5, $10 or $20, has to put a stamp on every cheque that he draws in order to get his own money out of the bank in which he has deposited it for safekeeping or as a matter of convenience.
Yes, the Bill imposes a stamp tax upon a transaction of that kind.
Does not my hon. friend appreciate the fact that that will prevent people from depositing their money in the bank? A man will not put money in the bank if he has to pay to get it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) will be able to tell my hon. friend (Mr. German) that there are probably more deposits than in any other place in the world in a tight little Kingdom in which the stamp tax has been known for a considerable time. We made pretty careful inquiries as to the effect of this tax, and it has been found that no such, untoward results as those feared by my hon. friend have ensued.

It is a very great pain to me to disagree with my deskmate (Mr. German), but I am bound to say that if a man puts money in the bank he does not put it in to take it out. He should leave it there and then he will only pay upon cheques when he issues to other people.

I have not very much to put there, but I will not put in any more if I have to pay to get it out.
(o) " Promissory note " does not include notes of a bank payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation.
You do not give any definition of a cheque as distinguished from an order. Is that necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think no such specific definition is required of the word "cheque." A cheque, of course, is a hill of exchange, but it has also a special, popular meaning as a bill of exchange 'drawn by one who has credit, or a deposit, with a financial institution. My Assistant Deputy informs me that in the Bills of Exchange Act, the word "cheque" has a definite meaning assigned to it.

I think there is a definition there, but my hon. friend has modified the usual definitions with reference to "bill of exchange" and "promissory notes." There might be confusion in regard to what would popularly be called an order. Take the case of a merchant doing a general business who receives orders as against either credit or actual money. Orders of this kind might be on his books to the credit of persons with whom he was doing business. Would each one of these orders, which, technically, are cheques, be subject to taxation? Technically, under the wider definition of the word "bank," a person who receives money and pays it out either in pursuance of an order or of a cheque would be within the meaning of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only thing we are taxing is a cheque drawn upon a bank as defined in the Act. A bill of exchange may be drawn upon A by B either for value received or in case A has an under. standing with B whereby he may avail himself of the credit he may thus obtain. We are imposing the Stamp Act upon a bill of exchange of that kind only i' it is negotiated through a bank. We apply the same principle in the case of a promissory note which, as my hon. friend knows, is different from a bill of exchange technically considered.

Take paragraph iv of section 12 and see how it works out in the actual business of the country. A bank is defined by paragraph iv of section 12 as 89
[DOT]-any one receiving money which he repays by honouring the cheques of the person from or on whose account the money was received.
Take the case of a solicitor or notary who might have in his hands a sum of money for distribution. The person who would be entitled to that money would give an order to some other person to receive it or there might be numerous orders. Technically, would that not come under the meaning of subsection 4; would not the custodian of the fund who paid it out be a person who had received money which he had repaid by honouring a cheque?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It refers to money paid
by a bank.
I refer to the definition of " bank " in subsection iv.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is intended to cover the case of an individual who is acting as a banker, who receives money on deposit which he repays by honouring the cheque of the person owning the money.
But it does not say " receiving money on deposit."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He pays cheques drawn
upon him.

That in ordinary
parlance is an order.

Do I understand that
drafts in the ordinary ' course of business would have to be stamped?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if they are negotiated through a bank.

They are all sent to
banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then they would be subject to the tax.
If I am administrator of an estate and I gave a cheque to the heirs, I would have to stamp the cheque?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if it is drawn on a bank.

What about promissory
notes of exchange between individuals that never go to a bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Notes between individuals not negotiated through a bank are not subject to the tax.
What about receipts as between individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are not subject to
the tax unless it be a receipt for money received from a bank.

Why should not the
notes between individuals be subject to the tax as well as those that go through a bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are a number of
transactions throughout the country in districts where they may not be aware of ithe law, and where the transactions are small, and it was thought they might be exempt on the ground of convenience. The revenue derived would be small and there would be great difficulty in enforcing the legislation.
Where will these stamps be on sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They will be on sale with postmasters and Inland Revenue officers, and others, as may be found necessary.
There are some sections of the country where there are no banks and it would be a great inconvenience to tax the people there.
The definition of the word "bank" is pretty wide; where is the limitation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 am informed that the definition here is the true legal definition of a bank.

I am not very clear as to how far that definition goes. I suppose that the words "any other body corporate" would apply to a trust company that receives deposits. Suppose I as a solicitor had money in my custody, and a person sends me an order which may be a cheque legally, would I be justified in refusing to pay that order or cheque unless there was affixed to it a stamp?'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite clear that a firm of solicitors would not be a bank under the provisions of the Act. If an order were given for payment by an individual, that order is not a cheque. A cheque is defined in the Bills of Exchange Act, and this Act as an instrument drawn upon a chartered bank, or upon a body corporate receiving money and honouring cheques for the person on whose account the money is received. An individual is a person who receives money which he retains to be honoured on a cheque. My hon. friend has no difficulty about a chartered bank and a corporate body which acts practically as a bank, but then we get to the case of the private banker, who may be in competition with a loan company, or a trust company, or a chartered bank. There are private banks in different

parts of the country which receive money on deposit, and they honour the cheques of their customers and under the English law they are undoubtedly carrying on a banking business, and we have sought by this definition to embrace them, because otherwise their customers would enjoy an advantage over the customers of banks and those other corporations which carry on practically a banking business. I can assure my hon. friend that there will be no attempt to enforce this Act as against a firm of solicitors acting merely on the order of some party to pay money, because that in my opinion would not be a cheque.

A practice exists in some of the eastern provinces where parties take a large number of promissory notes for articles sold at a sale, and they go to an individual to discount these notes which are usually for nine months or a year. Should the party who discounts these notes insist upon a stamp; would he be a banker within the meaning of the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. ,

Then there is no
reason why any one should not carry on the business of discounting notes without taking them to a bank at all, if he was able to recover them outside a bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a bank is not concerned the taxation is inoperative.
I quite agree with that, but the trouble is as to the limitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This refers only to an individual who receives money which may be paid by honouring a cheque, so that a cheque can be drawn upon him as a bank; in other words, a private banker. It is not intended to carry this further.

A man might not have his sign out that he is a private banker, but there are men who indulge in the business of what is called shaving notes, and the private individual to whom the notes are endorsed can go on without putting stamps on the notes which he receives.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He would not be a banker in my view; it would be a transaction between individuals.
On section 12, subsection 4-stamp tax on receipt for money paid by bank:

What particular
class of documents does the minister intend to reach by this subsection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Savings bank receipts. A
party goes into a bank and, instead of drawing a cheque in order to get money, he asks for a certain sum of money and gives a receipt for it. It is obvious that, unless we inserted this, we should lose revenue, because, instead of drawing a cheque, he would simply draw money and give a receipt. My assistant deputy minister tells me that that is the practice in some banks with regard to savings bank deposits. It is also the practice with certain loan companies carrying on a deposit business. They do not allow cheques to be drawn on them, but a customer goes in and asks for a certain sum of money and gives a receipt for it. It is a privilege, and we impose a stamp upon the receipt.

Does the subsection
apply to deposit receipts? In that case a customer does not sign a receipt, but endorses his deposit receipt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not apply to that.

What savings banks are
affected? There are two in Quebec, the City and District Savings Bank of Montreal, and the Caisse d'Economie de Notre Dame de Quebec. Are there any others?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say as to Quebec. There are a number of loan and trust companies in Toronto whose customers will be affected by this legislation. It is fairly general.
Will this include cooperative societies? There are some in Quebec and Ontario which receive deposits from their members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If they receive deposits
subject to cheque, it will.

Does this apply to
the Government Savings Bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Not being specifically mentioned, it would not be affected.
Does it apply to post office savings banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.
Subsection agreed to and section agreed to.
On section 12, subsection 7-issue of cheque without stamp:

I was not in the
House when the minister brought down this Bill in the morning. What arrangement 891
has been made to convenience the public in regard to issuing cheques so that one would not be liable to a penalty under the law? This legislation is to come into effect on the 15th of April. Throughout the country, in the different offices and in the hands of individuals, there are cheque books. It is-quite within the bounds of probability that a man might issue cheques out of those cheque books without thinking of stamps, and he would in that case be liable to a penalty under the law. How are those stamps to be made readily available?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have given consideration to that question, which is of great importance. I call the attention of my hon. friend to section 19, subsection 1 of which reads as follows:	'
The Minister, except as herein otherwise provided, may direct stamps to be prepared for the purposes of this Parliament of such kinds and bearing respectively such devices as he thinks proper, and all sums received for stamps and paper stamped by means of a die under this Parliament shall form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Then I call my hon. friend's attention to subsection 4 of section 19 in the Bill before him, which will become subsection 5 under an amendment which I intend to propose:
The minister may appoint any collectors of Inland Revenue, postmasters or other officers of the Government or other persons to sell stamps.
In addition to that provision, which we thought would readily enable the public to purchase stamps, we propose a further amendment, which I shall move when we come to section 19, as follows:
Postage stamps of the requisite value may in lieu of the stamps prepared under subsection 1 of this section be used in fulfilment and discharge of any requirement under this Parliament that adhesive stamps be affixed.
For the convenience of the public, if there is not ready at hand a war stamp so-called, a one-cent or a two-cent postage stamp may be used. Between now and the 15th of April we will endeavour to give as wide publicity as possible to the fact that this legislation will come into force on the 15th of April. While there may be some eases such as those that my hon. friend has in view, we hope that it will be fairly well-known by that time that this legislation is in force.
What is to be the design on the stamp?

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not had time to
turn my mind on that at all.

I do not think it wise in the interest of the country that we should be putting upon the statute-book laws which make certain actions crimes within the meaning of the law, where the operation of statutes of this kind could be obtained without the creation of an offence. The minister makes ample provision for the collection of this tax by providing that the banks must see that this stamp is on before the money is paid; but if my hon. friend constitutes a new crime in this country by declaring that a man for instance, who may be living some distance from a town, who has a cheque book in his possession and who issues a cheque without putting a stamp upon it any time after the 15th of April, shall be guilty of a crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A penalty.

The law will treat it as a crime; it will be as a matter of fact a crime. I am not captious in making the suggestion that we ought not to create a statutory crime if it can be avoided. Does not the minister sufficiently secure the collection of his tax by providing that the bank shall not cash cheques without a stamp, without creating this offence so that a person who may issue a cheque in good faith may be liable to be proceeded against under the wording of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows that in the case of one who acts in good faith and without knowledge of such legislation, it would be open to the magistrate to impose no penalty or a very small one. As in the case of all taxation there must be sanctions for its enforcement. I am given to understand by my assistant deputy that a penalty is enforced in other countries, in Great Britain for instance, in the case of stamp taxation. It is hardly probable that any hardship will arise. I would be willing to take into consideration the suggestion of my hon. friend that it will be sufficient to provide a penalty against one of .the parties, but I think it would be no harm to leave the section as it is so as to provide that there shall be a penalty for failure to put on a stamp not only on the part of the bank but on the part-of the drawer of the cheque, bill of exchange or promissory note. My present thought is that no harm will result from it and that it is an additional safeguard to the collection of our revenue.
I Mr. Marcil.]

I point to the danger which I see as a lawyer. Under section 20, subsection 3, the right is given to any one to proceed for penalties this part of the Act. Then, subsection 5 provides that
Any penalty collected and paid under part three may be divided with the person laying an information or otherwise aiding in effecting the conviction of the person accused, in such proportions as the Treasury Board in any case or class of cases directs and appoints.
The result is that prosecution may be instituted by one who is not an official representative of Government. I say it is unwise for Parliament to make what we might call an artificial crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before the reading of this Bill the third time, I shall be very glad to take into consideration the suggestion of my hon. friend.

Some time ago the Legislature of the province of Quebec passed an Act the effect of which was to compel incorporated companies to register in the court house. A number of companies, having other things to attend to, neglected to register. As a part of the fine went to the party who was the means of securing a conviction, many actions, known as qui tarn actions, were brought in Montreal for the recovery of the penalty. In this way a regular system of blackmail grew up. I am afraid that it will prove the same in this case if the Bill is passed in its present form. Unless the Government confines the penalty to the banks, I can see great danger of this evil arising.

I understand that this
will make no change in regard to the sale of ordinary postage-stamps, but in the case of stamps on cheques and notes,
4 p.m. sold by postmasters, the minister will lose 50 per cent of his revenue, because the postmasters get 50 per cent commission for the sale of stamps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same commission is given under this Bill for the sale of war stamps as for the sale of ordinary stamps.
Do I understand that letters mailed to foreign countries which are members of the Postal Union shall not require war stamps?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The postage plus the war
stamp must not exceed five cents. In the case of a letter directed to a party in the United States or Great Britain, an additional one-cent war stamp would be necessary.

The five-cent rate to
France will still remain at five cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where there is a five-cent rate now, no additional stamp tax is imposed.
Why should not the contractor or the person writing to the Government or to a department of Government on business, or peeking a job, he obliged to pay the extra war tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will observe that we are exempting letter- and postcards now entitled to the privilege of free transmission.

But why should you
do that? I agree that letters sent from the departments on Government or official business should be exempt; but take the contractor, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Take a member of this
House.

Take even a member,
if he is writing to a department when the House is not in session. But leaving out the members-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why leave out the members ?

Becauses when a member writes to a department of Government he usually does so in the interests of his constituents. On the other hand, when a contractor writes to the Government, invariably he does so in the interests of Mr. Contractor, and I do not see why he should not be obliged to pay the extra postage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Where the Post Office Act now provides for the free transmission of a letter or a post-card, it is obviously intended to be in the public interest, not in the interest of an individual. I cannot conceive that the existing legislation, which provides for the free transmission of letters, has in view the well-being of individuals. The provisions in question are designed in the public interest, the idea being that letters will be transmitted free when sent by any person to a minister or department of Government. The same argument would apply to the case of letters sent by members of this House. No individual interest is served; under this arrangement his constituents may receive letters, papers and *documents that they would not otherwise receive. I have no hesitation, therefore, in providing under this legislation for the
exemptions which are now made by the Post Office Act.
But you are changing the Post Office Act; you are increasing the postal rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not changing the
principle.

So far as the principle is concerned, I can understand why a member of the House writing letters on public business should not be obliged to-pay the extra tax, but why should the extra tax not be paid by a private person who is writing in his own interest? It may be argued that the amount collected in this respect would be so small that it would not be worth while re-drafting an amendment to cover the case, but I cannot see that any principle would exempt the contractor or private person in the case to which I have referred.

I am told that in the case of drop letters the extra tax may have the effect of decreasing rather than increasing the revenue. Large business concerns may employ messengers to deliver letters upon which they would have to pay two cents, whereas if the rate were one cent, as formerly, they would drop the letters in the post office. I should like to have the minister's view as to whether or not he expects to obtain a larger revenue through the imposition of the extra tax upon drop-letters than he would get if the old rate were continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The measure was considered! carefully by the Post Office Department and their opinion is that we shall receive a substantial increase in revenue from this source. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that open letters, or so-called circular letters, are not subject to the extra tax. I speak not with certainty, but I believe that the post. office has a monopoly in the distribution of letters, and while an individual may use his own service, I have doubt as to whether a service could be organized which would successfully compete with the post office.
Why are newspapers and the parcel post exempted from the operation of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it will be agreed that it is desirable that newspapers should be delivered to the public with as little expense as possible.
But in the case of newspapers mailed by individuals; why should the war stamp not be used in that case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose the same argument applies to newspapers as that which applies to open letters. I have great doubt as to whether we should increase the revenue in respect of so-called circular letters if we imposed a war stamp tax upon them. That is the view, I understand, of the Post Office Department.
I presume the same explanation applies to the exemption in respect of the parcel post?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We did have under consideration the question of imposing taxation on parcel post, but out of consideration for the public interest we determined that it would not be wise to impose such a tax.
This decision was not arrived at for departmental reasons, I presume?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
What is the meaning of the words "within Canada" in the second line of subsection 5?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This wording is taken from the Post Office Act. My hon. friend will observe that this provision applies to letters or postcards for transmission by post for any distance within Canada; therefore it would cover every letter posted in Canada.
No matter what their destination may be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No matter what their destination may be.
On section 13, subsection 6-distribution of prescribed stamps:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Subsection agreed to.
This section states that the Postmaster General Shall make arrangements for the distribution os postage stamps. What arrangements is it proposed that he shall make?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is also the language of the Post Office Act with regard to providing for the distribution of stamps. I think the language is very apt. The Postmaster General has officers throughout Canada; the arrangements he will make will be to supply them with stamps so that in turn they may supply the public.
Not to create new officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think not. I should think that the existing staff would be able to take care of it, but, if not, the staff would have to be increased.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Evidently my hon. friend has made up his mind to carry out his intention of requiring that two stamps shall be affixed to letters. This legislation, call it what you will, simply provides for increased postage. Why compel the people to affix to each of their letters two stamps instead of one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While we provide for & war tax stamp, we also provide, under the amendment made to section 19, that ordinary stamps may be used in the event of war stamps not being available. It is still the intention that a two-cent stamp shall be affixed to a letter where two cents is the postage, and that an additional one-cent stamp-not necessarily a war tax stamp-shall also be affixed.
Why not use a three-eent stamp instead of a two and a one ?
The war would be forgotten, perhaps, if there was not a war stamp; the Government wants to impress upon the public the fact that this tax is for war purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In view of my hon. friend's suggestion, I take it that it is his opinion that the fact should be impressed on the public, and that there should be a war tax stamp.
You say that the war tax stamp should be used, and then you say that the people need not use it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not say that they must use it. The Government thinks it advisable that a war stamp should be used in connection with this legislation. It is not the intention to increase the postal rate upon letters and postal cards. It may be said that in effect that is what we are <ioing, but what we are doing is to provide a war stamp on account of the war. If there were no war, this war tax would not be imposed.
If the war ceases in June, will the tax -cease -also ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The tax will not cease
automatically, but it would not be the object of this or of any other Government to continue special taxation longer than is necessary. As to what time in the future the necessity for its imposition will cease, I am unable to say. I cannot forecast the future so far as the war is con-

MARCH 24, 19i5
cerned-its contingencies, vicissitudes, or duration-nor do I know what the situation may be when the war is at an end.
Is it intended to continue the collection of this tax after the war is over ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hesitate to give an expression of intention at the present time, because I do not know how long the war is going to last.
You do not know how long the Government is going to be in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a better idea as to that than I have as to how long the war will last. If this taxation, however, were to remain in force throughout the incumbency of the present Government, I am afraid there might be a protest against it on the ground of its lasting so long. With regard to this special taxation, which is imposed to meet the exigency of the war, I think it has been the principle of governments generally not to continue special taxation in effect longer than is necessary. Naturally, at the end of a war they have to consider the situation which is left by the war, and it would be extremely unwise to make any statement in advance as to what a government would do when a war comes to an end. What any government is obliged to do when a war comes to an end is to consider the situation that then confronted it and to deal with that situation as may seem proper. It would be unwise, therefore, for me to make any statement as to what the Government will or will not do, except this: that no government desires to continue special taxation in effect longer than is absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is not the point. The House has resolved by solemn vote that there shall be an increase in postage. Call it war tax, or call it what you will; the fact remains that the postal rates are increased. But why subject those who use the facilities offered by the post office to the vexatious proceeding of affixing two stamps to a letter instead of one? Why not have one three-cent stamp? But my hon. friend is not satisfied with that; he wants everybody to put the usual two-cent stamp on his letter and to affix also a one-cent stamp bearing the words " war-tax." Is that not a vexatious proceeding? Everybody knows that this is a war tax, so-called; why subject the people to extra inconvenience? My hon. friend says the Government will be a long time in office,
but I suggest to him that the electors will damn the Government, if I may use the expression, because of their being compelled to adopt this inconvenient and vexatious procedure. My hon. friend cannot deny that the issue and sale of a three-cent stamp would be the most convenient method of collecting the tax, but he wants to impose this useless proceeding upon the public simply to make it appear that this is a war tax.

Another advantage of the three-cent stamp is that it would be in keeping with the Conservative policies of former days, when taxation was three cents. It would remind the people that they are back to the old system.

If, as the minister says, the object of the war stamp is to keep the public alive to the fact that this tax is due to the war, why does this section not state that there shall be impressed on the stamp the words " war tax " ? Why say " may " ?
It might be difficult for parties sending letters, or making use of war stamps under the provisions of this Act, to obtain those war stamps notwithstanding the wide distribution that will be accomplished by the Inland Revenue Department. Therefore, it is provided by an amendment to section 19 that postage-stamps of the requisite value may be used in lieu thereof.
That is only until the others are ready.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I make a change in section 19 by providing that postage-stamps may
