be used in lieu thereof. It is for the public convenience. My right hon. friend has spoken of the trouble and inconvenience which will be occasioned the public if we make them put on these stamps. I do not agree with Mm. My right hon. friend is sitting in the cool shades of Opposition and he will continue to adorn the Opposition benches, I hope, for many years to come. If we do not complain about putting on an additional stamp I do not believe that my hon. friend, who has nothing to do except criticise, should complain about being obliged to do the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not the Government I pity; it is the electors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend's pity is wasted on the electors because the electors in time of war will not complain about putting on an additional stamp. I think the public will gladly put on the stamp, and they will be pleased to use the war stamp tax instead of the ordinary stamp that we are permitting them to put on. The hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) suggested that we were going back to the old system. It must be gathered from what he said the other day that he would like the impression to go out that this Government is raising the postage upon letters. We are not raising the postage upon letters.
The effect is the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The effect may be the same, but that is not precisely what we are doing. We are allowing the postage to remain as it is and we are providing that a war stamp shall be placed upon each letter and a tax collected in that way upon each letter. There is a difference between the two things. If we use a three-cent stamp or a two-cent stamp instead of a two and a one, or two ones respectively, my hon. friend would represent that we had raised the postage. We have not raised the postage. We are imposing a special tax upon all letters which will be gladly paid by the people of this country in order to assist the Dominion to do its share in carrying on this war, and I do not believe that the public will complain. I do not believe that my hon. friend writes sufficient letters to put him to any particular inconvenience. If it is a difficult thing for him to moisten these stamps, because he referred to it the other day, why he has his secretary. There is no reason why he should have to discharge that

unpleasant task; or he could get a moistener.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not want to impose upon my secretary what I do not like to do myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will get my right hon. friend a moistener.
Does the Bill provide that the stamps shall be supplied at the post office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I understand that you can use an ordinary one-cent stamp instead of a war stamp?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
If a man put on two one cent war stamps and a one cent regular stamp, what effect will that have?
There will be more licking still.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My deputy, who has given close attention to the matter of this legislation, assures me that this letter would be sufficiently stamped.
Does the minister take power to recall this stamp tax by proclamation, or must he wait for the meeting of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no power taken to recall this tax. It will remain in effect until next session at least.

I do not think this clause should pass with the last remark which the committee had from the minister. He says that this is not an addition to the postage. That is a very bold position to take up. War is an incident in the history of a country, just as much as a bad or extravagant Government is an incident in the history of a country, and whether, because of war or of an extravagant Government-I am taking a suppositious case- you may have to impose addiional taxes. In Britain or in any other country one has seen taxes raised as a result of war or from some other cause, but when an additional penny was put on the income tax, was it in order for the Chancellor of the Exchequer to get up and say: This is not an addition to the income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this is a tax.
This is a war tax, but my hon. friend says it is not an addition to the postage.
Neither is it.

You pay three cents on a letter instead of two, and yet you say it is not an addition to the postage? It is perfectly open to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to say that this additional postage is for the purpose of raising a revenue for war, but to say it is not additional postage is to say something which verges very closely upon nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In subsection 5 of section 13 my hon. friend from Red Deer may read the following:
On every letter and post card for transmission by post for any distance within Canada and on every letter and post card not Intended for transmission through the mails but for posting and delivery at the same post office, there shall be levied and collected a tax of one cent.
That is a tax; it is not a charge for postal service.
I was not dealing with that at all; I was dealing with the language which I think Hansard will prove the minister used. It is not additional postage, he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not additional postage; it is a tax.

All postage stamps are taxes. .
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER: The name by which you call it makes no difference; it smells no better.
Do I understand that the department will keep a separate account of the moneys that are collected on war stamps and on regular postage stamps?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As far as we can.

My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) asked if you could use an ordinary one cent stamp instead of a war stamp, and the minister said "yes>" and he also said that a two cent stamp and a one cent stamp would be good enough, or that three ones would be good enough. Ordinarily the whole of the money derived from postage stamps accrues to the Post Office Department. If three one cent stamps are used instead of a two cent stamp and a war stamp, the whole of the money goes to the Post Office Department and stays there. Therefore, I cannot see what this is except an increase in the charge for the carrying of letters. The present idea is that there is a quid pro quo. You have a letter to be sent from Sydney to British Columbia, and the contract you have with the Post Office Department is that they will carry your letter to British Columbia for
two cents. If you put three war stamps on the post office gets nothing at all. It carries the letter for nothing, the idea being that all the money collected is a tax, and the department gets no quid pro quo for carrying your letter, but if the charge is three cents for carrying your letter, then it is simply the old contract made a little clearer to the people. I think the distinction is rather finer than the ordinary man will understand. It would be more convenient if the sender of a letter were obliged to put only a three cent stamp on, instead of being compelled to carry two sets of stamps to be put on the one letter.
Is the minister advised by the experts of the Post Office Department that the volume of letters will remain as it is to-day, or will there be a falling off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My advice from the Post Office Department is that the imposition of additional taxation on closed letters and postcards would result in a very substantial increase in the revenue,

It should
not be difficult to keep the accounts separate so as to be able to determine how much is paid as war tax and how much for ordinary postage. If this were done I think it would be found that the business of the Postmaster General has gone down, and that the business of the Minister of Militia, who is the embodiment of war, has improved vastly, because it will be the war tax stamps and not postage stamps that will be put on letters. What means will be taken to show what is war tax and what is ordinary postage rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will have to be a matter of estimate by the Post Office Department. By reason of the provision that the postage stamp may be used in lieu of the war tax stamp, the accounts could not be kept separately. There will have to be an estimate made by the Post Office Department.
It can only be a guess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should say it would be a very likely guess.

Will three war stamps
carry a letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Three war stamps would
carry a letter and the postage would be credited with two.
What is the percentage allowed the postmasters for selling stamps?

Fifty per cent up to
one thousand dollars; thirty per cent from one thousand to ten thousand dollars; and twenty per cent above ten thousand dollars.

You impose a penalty of one hundred dollars on an express company which issues a money order or cheque without a stamp, or which fails to cancel the stamp. That seems drastic. Suppose an express company accidentally neglected to affix a stamp, would the company be liable to a penalty of one hundred dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The company would be liable according to the statute, but no doubt if it were sought to impose the penalty the court would have regard to all the circumstances.
Why not insert the words "or who wilfully neglects to affix the stamp?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be gross negligence [DOT]on the part of an express company to issue a money order without a stamp; we must assume that the company would carry out the provisions of the Act.
Suppose in the hurry of business they were issuing a number of express orders and the company omitted to stamp one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An express company is a public service corporation, and if it makes a mistake it should pay for it.

Why not provide that the penalty shall not exceed *one hundred dollars, or any sum you like to state, and then leave it to the court to determine according to the evidence what the fine should be. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of persons who are liable to a penalty we fix the penalty at an amount not exceeding a certain sum; but in the case of an express company, if it makes a mistake we want it to-'pay one hundred dollars. We want to ensure that it will not make a mistake, because there is no reason why a company organized as an express company is should make a mistake.	[DOT]
Then, in that case you should make the penalty five hundred dollars, because a company can pay five hundred dollars for its mistake more easily than a person can pay fifty dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If an express company is fined for an infraction of this section, it will make it more careful.
Would it not be more logical to fix a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars or a thousand dollars if you like, and then the magistrate in his decision could decide what the penalty should be.

Will the war tax stamp and the ordinary postage stamp be combined? Suppose a postmaster sells a thousand dollars' worth of ordinary postage stamps he would be entitled to a commission of five hundred dollars, and then if he sells five hundred dollars' worth of war tax stamps, he would be entitled to a remuneration of two hundred and fifty dollars, if they are kept separate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The two will be added together.
I would point out to the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) that he has not yet asked the minister whether people will have to pin on the stamps instead of licking them.
Does my hon. friend suggest that we should keep all the licking for the Germans.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is only a pin-prick.
I would like to have an expression of opinion from the minister as to the penalties mentioned in sections 10 and 11. Does the minister understand that the court has no discretion in these cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The intention there is, in the case of an express company, that there is no discretion, and that it incurs a penalty of one hundred dollars if it violates the provisions of the statute.

I register a complaint against that because after all a corporation is nothing except an entity which has no personality, and the minister must not forget that the corporation will fall back upon some individual clerk in the long run, and if that clerk makes a mistake he will have to pay the hundred dollars and likely lose his position as well. It is hitting at some poor clerk who may make a mistake and not at the larger shareholders. Discretion should be left with the court in a case of that kind as in any other case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the general statutes I
understand there is discretion with the

Governor in Council to deal with particular cases of penalties. Apart from that, the Bank Act provides that a bank, for failing to comply with the provisions of the Act, becomes liable to a penalty. The principle should be different in the case of individuals from that in the case of institutions such as express companies. If an individual violates this legislation, discretion should be left with the magistrate as to whether he will impose the maximum penalty or not. If on the other hand an express company, which is organized for the purpose of doing the business to which we refer here, fails to carry out the provisions of this Bill-and it is very necessary that there should be penalties to ensure their proper carrying out-the imposition of a penalty of $100 is not extreme. That is my view; but I shall be gl~d to take into consideration the suggestion of my hon. friend, who has had a good deal of experience in the matter of imposition of penalties under the criminal law, with a view of seeing whether the penalty should be modified or not. At present my view is that it should be allowed to stand. I will take the matter into consideration between the present time and the third reading of the Bill.
How are stamps cancelled on express orders? There does not seem to be any definition of the word " cancel."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a definition of the word " cancel " later on in the Bill.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Postmaster General to a suggestion made at the beginning of this session by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who unfortunately is very ill. I understand that letters coming from the boys at the front now come into Canada free of postage. His idea is that letters mailed from Canada to the boys in the trenches should also go free. Has the Government given that matter any consideration ? The other night I moved a resolution in regard to that, and I allowed it to stand at the request of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in the absence of ft he Postmaster General, and at the request of the Prime Minister, who stated that the matter had not been considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter comes more particularly under the jurisdiction of the Postmaster General, and I should not like to express an opinion on it, because I have
not looked into ilt, nor have I had it before me in any way.

We have considered the question, and it was our desire to facilitate as much as possible the sending of mail to the soldiers at the front. We found this difficulty in the way, namely, that the mail would be carried not only by the postal authorities of Canada, but by the postal authorities of Great Britain and of France. Therefore we would have to have some arrangement with the postal authorities of Great Britain and of France. That arrangement we have not tried to make, because we did not think we would succeed.
Is not the attempt worth while ? I am sure it woidd be appreciated.

Members of this House and officials of the different departments send letters to France that go free, the Government putting the stamp on so far as that country is concerned. If it is considered desirable to grant the same privilege in respect of letters going to our boys at the front, I do not see why it could not be done..
Must this alleged war stamp be put on letters which are franked or on letters going to Canadian soldiers abroad on foreign service? If so, it seems to be rather anomalous that the friends of our boys who axe fighting the battle of Canada in the trenches, should have to place a war stamp on letters which they send to them. The suggestion of my hon. friend the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), which has been supported by my hon. friend the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), that letters mailed	to our soldiers	inthe trenches	should go free	of
postage and also free of this war stamp, should be carried out. Is this war tax intended to apply to all letters which are franked, that is to say to letters which are sent by or to members of Parliament or the different departments of the Government? I think it should apply to them, but I am inclined to think that the. Bill in its present form will not make it apply. Those who are entitled to frank their letters today will be able under this Bill to send them free of the war stamp tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend was out of the House when that matter was rather fully discussed a little while ago. He is correct in his conclusion that, under the provisions of this Bill, the tax of one cent
142(

imposed in addition to the postage shall not be levied or collected on any letter or post card entitled to the privilege of free transmission under the provisions of the Post Office Act.
Is that an amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is in subsection 5 of section 13 of the Bill. I pointed out-and it is not necessary for me to amplify my remarks in view of the fact that the discussion took place in the House a little while ago-that the exemptions under the present Post Office Act are by reason of considerations of public interest. The reason why letters are allowed to be transmitted free is not in the interest of individual members of this House so much, as in the interest of the public, in order that members may send not only letters, but papers and documents to their constituents. The provision for free transmission of letters to the departments of the Government was, 'I think, originally conceived on the same principle, namely, out of consideration for the public interest and not out of consideration for the particular individual who happened to be communicating with the Government. That answers, so far as I can answer, the last question propounded to me by my hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley).
To come to the question of letters addressed to soldiers-my hon. friend says " in the trenches "[DOT]-he knows that the Government, as has been pointed to the House, is putting itself behind the soldiers in the trenches. Personally, I should be of opinion that the friends and relatives of the soldiers would be only too glad to pay the additional war tax, knowing that it is provided for the purpose of enabling this Government to better support the soldier in the trenches. To ease the mind of my hon. friend, if he has any doubt about it, I pointed out a little time ago that, by reason of another provision in this Act, namely, that the tax is not to be levied if contrary to the Universal Postal Convention, this war stamp tax does not apply on letters on which postage of five cents is required. In other words a letter sent to France, five cents postage being necessary, will not have to bear the war stamp tax, because five cents is the limit under the Universal Postal Convention.

The minister will understand that the Government gets no credit for that, because it is out of their power
[Mr. W. T. White.!
under the terms of the convention, to impose a tax on a letter going to France. I thought this question of sending letters free of tax to the soldiers was not a party question, but would be approved by the House, especially as the letters from the soldiers come free of postage. That being so why cannot one who receives a letter from a soldier at the front have the same advantage in answering?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another question.
I may tell the Postmaster General-perhaps he does not know-that letters sent by Canadian soldiers and coming to Canada are. free of postage. Why cannot the reply also go free of postage?

Perhaps I may be allowed a word here and then the Minister of Finance can answer both my hon. friend and me. The hon. minister says that I may free my mind of any anxiety with regard to letters to Canadian soldiers in France being obliged to bear the stamp tax because the postage on letters to France is five cents, and in consequence of the Universal Postal Union arrangement no postage beyond five cents can be collected. Does that apply in this case? The minister has told us that this is not postage; that this is a war tax. That being so, the International Postal Convention would have no application. So, if the minister wanted to exempt such letters from tax he should have a section in the Bill especially providing for it. He cannot depend on the International Postal Convention, according to his own argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We gave consideration to
the views the hon. gentleman has put forward which are rather obvious to one who considers the matter. There is no doubt that this is not additional postage; it is a war tax imposed upon letters. But even if it were as clear as noonday that the Government had the right to impose this war tax upon letters in addition to the postage without violation of the Universal Postal Convention, my view would be that the Government should not impose it. And we do not propose to impose it; we propose that the postage plus the taxation shall not exceed five cents. At the same time I would say what I have said, I think, at least a dozen times before-expressing my own view of course, and my hon. friend is quite open to put forward his view in contradiction-that this is a war stamp tax.

It is so stated in the Bill and is so intended; it would not be imposed unless war existed. So far as I am concerned, arid without disrespect to my hon. friend, I will not discuss what I consider a quibble any further. It is a war stamp tax, and it seems to me it is idle to discuss that question.

Quibble or no quibble, I run not discussing that question. I am assuming that it is a war tax, that it is not a payment for postal service. Thus I am giving the hon. minister the full benefit of what he says. If, then, this does not increase the postage, the Universal Postal Union regulations have no application to the case. But the minister says that the Government does not intend to accept anything beyond the five cents, and where the postage is five cents and is paid on a letter, as in the case of letters for
5 p.m. France, there will be no further war stamp tax imposed. What I would like to know is whether there is anything in the Bill which so provides. If there is not, then the Government is going to do what, in my opinion, it has no power to do; it is going to act contrary to the statute, for it will pass a regulation which the Act gives the Government no power to pass. What the Government ought to do is to provide for that in the Bill. If the Minister is not going to regard this as a mere quibble, but as something that members of this House have a right to inquire about, I would like to know where in this Bill authority is given to the Government to exempt from the stamp tax a letter with a five-cent, stamp upon it from the stamp tax? It may be in the Bill, hut I have not seen it there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no objection to giving the matter consideration and getting the opinion of the Justice Department. My own view is that it would be impossible to impose this additional tax, if in substance and in spirit it is opposed to the Universal Postal Convention, in other words, if the postage of five cents is exceeded. If there is anything in the draft,-ihg inconsistent with that-but I do not think there is-I will reconsider the drafting.
Perhaps the assistant-deputy could inform the minister where the provision is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Subsection 5 of section 13 is as follows:
Such tax shall not be levied or collected on any letter or post-card entitled to the privilege of free transmission under the provisions of the Post Office Act, nor on any letter or post card if the levying and collecting of such tax would be contrary to the provisions of the Universal Postal Convention concluded between Canada and certain other countries.
That, is to say, if the levy is contrary to the provisions, then it will not he made I do not believe that language more proper to express the meaning could be found.
"If it is contrary?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a question of fact and of law. So far as this Bill, which will become a statute, is concerned, it is perfectly clear that if it is in conflict with the Universal Postal Convention, then the tax will not be imposed. If, on the other hand, it is not in conflict with the terms of the postal union, then the tax could be imposed.
Will it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a question which
we will consider in due course. In the meantime, this Bill is perfectly clear in that if the tax would be a violation of the terms of the postal union, it will not be levied and collected.
That is clear, if the imposition of the tax would be a violation, but it is not clear that it would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suggest that the hon.
member look the matter up and come to a conclusion for himself.

I will do that if my hon. friend will promise to put into legislation my suggestions in the matter, but what is the good of my looking it up? The responsibility is not on me; it is on the Government. I repeat that it is clear that if the tax would be a contravention of the postal union, it cannot be imposed, but it is not clear that the imposition of the tax would be a violation of the terms of the postal union. If the Minister of Finance holds to the view that this is not postage at all, but simply a tax which, for convenience, is collected through the sale of postage stamps, then the exaction of the tax would not be a contravention of the universal postal union. However, if my hon. friend will look into the matter, that is all I ask.
Do I understand that the Government's decision in the matter of free letters to soldiers is final?

I am sorry the hon.
gentleman is putting that question now; it is a matter which is engaging the attention of the department. As I said before; it is our wish to send letters free to the soldiers at the front, if it is at all possible and consistent with the necessities and requirements of the Post Office Department. I may supplement the information which I gave the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) respecting the vending of stamps by saying that when stamps are sold in post office lobbies, the remuneration to the vendor is up to two cents on the dollar. In other words, the allowance made to those who sell stamps in post office lobbies is up to two cents on the dollar, according to the discretion of the postmaster. In cases where stamps are sold by druggists and others, their renumeration is one cent on the dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Without intending to prolong the discussion-because the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has intimated that he is satisfied with my saying that we shall be glad to give the matter consideration-I would call his attention to the fact that in the postal convention, article 5, the English version is " the rates of postage," whereas the French version is " les taxes." This circumstance must be borne in mind in giving consideration to the question as to whether this provision of the Bill now under consideration is a violation of the convention.
But the minister has said that it is not a tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Both seem to be provided for here, and that would lend strength to tlhe view which I expressed that the rate of five cents should not be exceeded, because in the French version the expression is " les taxes."

The hon. minister will remember that when a gentleman on this side spoke of postage as a tax, he said that it was not a tax; that postage was a consideration for the performance of the service. He said, however, that this war stamp tax is something entirely different. My hon. friend cannot blow hot and cold at the same time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
On section 14, subsection 1-consumers:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yesterday I raised the question as to our power to tax champagne, having regard to the French

treaty. My hon. friend told me that he would consult the Department of Justice in the matter; has he done so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall read tne opinion of the Department of Justice, which I have obtained in pursuance of the right hon. gentleman's request. It is as follows:
Ottawa, 23rd March, 1915.
Dear Mr. Ross,-Referring to your letters of 19th and 20th instant, submitting a question as to whether the imposition of stamp duties upon wines as proposed by the Special War Revenue Act, 1915, Bill conflicts with the French Convention scheduled to chapter 28 of the Acts of 1908, and in which you allude to a contention that there may he special ground for immunity of champagne because it is not like a product of Canadian origin, and state moreover that you are advised that there are concerns in Canada manufacturing what they call champagne and selling it as such, I may say that upon the best consideration which I have been able to give to the subject the proposed legislation does not conflict with the stipulations of the convention. It will be perceived that the stamps are required to be attached only upon sale unless the importer be also the consumer, in which case the stamps must be affixed after importation and while the wine is in customs. It was agreed by article V of the Convention that certain French wines should upon their importation into Canada enjoy the benefit of stipulated customs duties, and it was moreover in effect provided by article XII that these wines when imported into Canada shall not be subject to any other duties of exicse, internal consumption or octroi than those which are or may be charged upon like products of Canadian origin. The tax now proposed is not, as I have shown, a tax upon importation, but a tax to which native wines are subject equally with imported wines. It is an excise or Inland revenue tax as distinguished from a customs tax, and it is 1 think intended to be imposed in strict conformity wtih the obligations undertaken by the convention. Indeed I do not see how it can be contended that these stamp duties in their general character can be aptly included within any proper definition of customs duties. Whether or not Canada produces or can produce any wine corresponding to " les grands vins de champagne" may of course be very doubtful, but it appears that Canada does produce a wine sufficiently like champagne to bear its name and have many of the same qualities. It may also be observed that the stamp duty of twenty-five cents a pint is imposed not upon champagne alone but upon sparkling wines generally, Irrespective of the place of origin, and sparkling wines are I believe admittedly produced in Canada. But independently of this question I do not find any clause in the convention intended to exempt French wines from duties of excise or internal consumption upon the ground that like wines are not produced in Canada, but I think that if any such intention existed it should have been expressed or at least necessarily implied by the language used. I do not see any necessary implication in article XII, and this question is referable only to that article.
Yours faithfully,
E. D. Newcombe.

In connection with this opinion I have here a card of the Pelee Island Wine and Vineyard Company, and I find that they advertise for sale, among other wines and liquors, a registered brand of champagne "extra dry" and "sec." cases, 12 quarts, $18; cases, 24 pints, $20. There seems no doubt, as the Deputy Minister of Justice has stated, that sparkling wines are manufactured in Canada. I give this information because it may be useful to the committee in considering the opinion which I have just read upon the subject.
The minister refers to medicines manufactured by any occult art. The dictionary describes witchcraft as an occult art, and I wondered why the minister found it necessary to use the word in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: "Occult" means hidden, not disclosed. I would not say that the word was exclusively confined to witchcraft or any of the allied arts. It is of much more liberal application that to the art of witchcraft. Its general meaning is "not divulged or made public," and that is the meaning we have in mind.
Then coloured water passed off as medicine would be liable to the tax?

Occult sciences are defined in the dictionary as follows:
Those sciences of the middle ages which relate to the influence of occult qualities or supernatural powers, as magic, necromancy, alchemy, witchcraft, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the narrow meaning.
On section 15-stamp tax on patent medicines, perfumery and wines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an amendment which will consist in the insertion of a new subsection 3 and the changing of the present subsection 3 to subsection 4. The amendment is necessitated on this account. It has been found that there are certain wine growers who, operating under licenses of the Inland Revenue Department, use the wine which they produce in making some sort of medicinal preparation, the resultant not being subject to any special tax. As the Bill stood on first reading it was only when wines were sold to a consumer that they became subject to a tax. A subsection has been added to section 15 to meet this case, under which every producer of wines who uses his productions in producing some other article of value has to pay the tax. The new subsection will read as follow:
3. Every manufacturer or producer of - (a) a proprietary or patent medicine (b) perfumery (c) wine of the grape, non-sparkling or (d) champagne or sparkling wine, who is a consumer, shall, under regulations made by the minister, before using any such article in producing therefrom any other article of value, affix an adhesive stamp of the requisite value as mentioned in the schedules of this part, to the bottle or packages containing such article.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood from my hon. friend that is to apply simply to wine growers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can my hon. friend give any idea of the nature of the article of value produced? Is it a medicine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be a medicine. *

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There are certain wines called medicinal wines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is it.

I wish to raise my protest against the tax which is proposed to be put on proprietary medicines. I do not see any reason why there should be a tax on them any more than on the prescription that a person takes to a druggist and has filled. I do not think medicines should be taxed, even for war purposes. A man gets medicine when he is sick; he does not take it as a luxury as he does champagne or candy; and the Government are proposing to hamper the man who is sick in his endeavour to get well. Besides his doctor's bill he is being hampered with the payment of a tax on a patent medicine which many people believe to be more efficient in aiding recovery than even the doctor's prescription.
Mr.- WHITE:	This legislation is not a
precedent in the taxation of proprietary medicines; it exists in other countries. Wherever an exclusive right, or monopoly, exists where large profits are made-although that is not universally true in the case of patent or proprietary medicines- there is a proper field for taxation. Taxa tion in other countries to which I have alluded has not been regarded as a hardship on the community, nor do I believe that the imposition of these taxes will be seriously objected to. There are numerous exceptions to this taxation. It occurred to me that in the case of patent or proprietary medicines, for which an exclusive rigid to manufacture exists or where a patent or proprietary article is held up to the public as being a specific or cure-all, the state might very well say that a tax must be

paid for the right. Governments continually impose taxes upon people for the right to exercise certain callings. Doctors have to pay fees before they are permitted to practise their profession and lawyers are in the same category. If a vendor holds it up to the public that he is selling a specific or cure-all, if he is representing himself to be a physician, I see no reason why a small tax should not be paid to the state for the privilege. Patent medicine proprietors are practically permitted to exercise the calling of a physician.

The great difficulty I see with my hon. friend's argument is that he is assuming continually that the vendor of the patent medicine is the man who will pay the tax. He is not the man who will pay the tax at all. It will be the sick man who buys the medicine in order to improve his health. He is the man who will pay the tax, and it will be burdensome to him. If the manufacturer of the patent medicine had to pay the tax, and it was to come out of him exclusively and not out of the man who is ill and requires nourishing treatment, there would be something in the hon. gentleman's argument. The hon. gentleman imposes a tax, and the statute, in its very terms, says practically that the purchaser is the one who shall pay the tax, because the stamp is only to be attached to the commodity at the time of sale to the consumer, not to the retail druggist, but to the man who desires a medicine, whatever it may be-not a cure-all-but a specific, for the treatment of a certain disease.
. Mr. MAROIL: For man or beast.

For man or beast, as my hon. friend suggests. It is not a cure-all, but a specific for some particular ailment which happens to afflict the man at the time. He has to pay the tax. It is an injustice to, and an imposition upon, a large class of the community.

As between the hon.
Minister of Finance and my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) I should say that the fair way to have imposed taxation on these medicines would have been to have stipulated that there should be no increase in the price to the consumer. Patent medicines, I understand, have a very large margin of profit. Prescriptions, I understand, are exempt from taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A compound made from a doctor's prescription is not taxed. It is not a proprietary medicine.
What would happen if a doctor prescribed a proprietary medicine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he prescribes a patent or a proprietary medicine and it is purchased, there is no doubt that the stamp tax will be payable. But if, on the other hand, a proprietary medicine is used as part of a mixture compounded from a doctor's prescription, then the mixture is different in character from the proprietary medicine which forms a part of it, and there will be no tax payable upon that compound or mixture.

The minister has not answered the argument of my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German). The argument is that there is no good reason why a man who uses a patent medicine should be taxed, while the man who takes a doctor's prescription should go free. The reason why a man uses patent medicines is generally that he cannot afford to get a doctor's prescription. The patent medicine is the poor man's medicine. The minister ought to consider that question, and show us a good reason why he imposes a tax on patent medicines and refrains from imposing a tax on medicine that is prescribed by a physician. I agree with my hon. friend from Welland, and I wish to record my protest against this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is assuming that the public will bear the whole of this tax.
There is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing in the Act that makes that clear. Presumably patent medicines and perfumes are selling now at as high a price that they tean be sold at. How that tax will be borne, and what its incidence will be, neither I nor any one else can quite tell. My own view is that it will probably be absorbed by the different interests concerned. A slight part of it may possibly be paid by the public, a part may be paid by the wholesaler, and a part may be paid by the manufacturer. The incidence of the tax cannot quite be forecasted. We will have to wait the result of the taxation to find that out. We may not be able to find it out accurately, even after the measure has been in force for some time, but my hon. friend is considering it from the hypothesis that the consumer will have to pay the whole of this tax. I do not agree with him.
I think there is no doubt about it.

I think the minister expresses himself most accurately when he says that he is imposing a tax and does not know where it is going to strike. The Government have done that with regard to the whole of the tariff resolutions. They have made a horizontal increase in the tariff, and I venture to say that they do not know how it is going to affect the revenue or what interests it will affect beneficially or detrimentally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In regard to the horizontal increase, I can tell my hon. friend that if he opposes it in his own constituency, it will strike him.
I can tell the minister that I am not afraid of the horizontal increase or of him either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will strike him. Speaking generally in regard to taxation, either direct or indirect, it is not quite possible to say precisely or accurately just upon whom it will fall. We have our opinion that it will fall in a certain way. But any tax has some uncertainty in its incidence. My own view is that this tax may be absorbed, and that the public will only have to pay, if any, a very small part of it.

The minister makes a statement which seems to me to be somewhat extraordinary. He says that if my hon. friend from Welland takes an independent position in Welland, this horizontal increase of the tariff will strike him in that district. Perhaps the minister will he good enough to explain what he means by that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My language is perfectly clear.
Is it because the horizontal increase is a protective tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend keeps on guessing.

I cannot imagine any other reason than that. Then the minister lets the cat out of the hag when he says that the tariff is not merely to raise a revenue, but it is for the purpose of protection. My hon. friend's constituency is a manufacturing district, and therefore if he has the independence to raise his voice in this Parliament against what he himself believes to be an unjust tariff, it is going to strike him because the manufacturers will resent it. That is what my hon. friend's statement means if it means anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Among the arguments used by hon. gentlemen opposite against this 90
taxation was that it might incidentally assist the " Made-in-Canada " movement, and if my hon. friend would get up in his constituency and belittle the made-in-Canada movement, I think he would not be advantaged politically.

The greatest opponent of the made-in-Canada movement is the minister himself, because he deplores the depression which exists in Canada because we have not imports. He has himself, in paragraph after paragraph, explained that he has not income sufficient for his wants because we have not been importing so much as we were importing, and he has deplored the loss of revenue and the necessary resort to taxation in consequence. So that when he taunts any one of us with being the opponent of the made-in-Canada movement, I do not think he understands our position; I am sure he does not understand mine. I claim him as being in agreement with me unless he says that the cutting off of exports was a good thing, and that the loss of revenue was a good thing. I do not understand his Budget statement in that sense.

Then too, we all remember in 1912, when the Minister of Finance made his Budget speech and when this country was going forward under the momentum it had received during the years of prosperity when the Liberal Government was in power, how the Minister of Finance rejoiced at the increase in imports and the consequent increase in revenue. The hon. gentleman took a very different position then from that which he takes now. As has been said by my hon. friend from Red Deer, the hon. gentleman knows he cannot have revenue unless he has imports. The Minister of Finance has justified the tax on patent medicines upon the ground that many of these patent medicines are owned by those who have made a good deal of money in the past, and when he is driven into a corner-if you will pardon me for using that expression, but it is not quite so offensive as the word " quibble " which he used- when he is driven into a corner-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By whom?

By the fallacy of hi* arguments; by the fact that he has made most fallacious arguments in support of this tax upon proprietary and patent medicines. When he is driven into a corner he is obliged to admit that he doesn't know whether this tax is going to be



borne by the sick man and the poor man who uses these patent medicines, or by the manufacturer. If it is to be borne by the consumer, then I say, as other hon. gentlemen have said, that it is a burden upon the poor man and upon the sick man. It is only the sick who use these medicines, as a rule; of course they may use them when they are not very sick, but it is sick people and poor people who use patent medicines, as a rule. These medicines are largely used by people in the country diS' triets who live a distance away from a medical man and find it 'desirable to have relief against pain. It does seem to m? that the protest of my hon. friend (Mr. German) is properly made, and it certainly ought to be considered by this Government. They ought to pause before they add still further to the burdens which are placed upon the masses of the people of this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This says
that cancellation may be made by writing initials, or "other marks of identification" across the stamp. What is the meaning of those words?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is regarded as a
necessary safeguard to the Inland Revenue, and it is taken from the English Act. If there is any suggestion that will simplify the cancellation and at the same time guard the revenue, I would be glad to consider it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Up to the present in this Bill, we have provided, as should be provided, that all stamps should be erased, and the method hitherto provided has been by putting on the initials of the party who has to do the erasing, and the date, but here you give an alternative when you use the words "or any other mark of identification."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A provision similar to this ran through the Act before and we changed it by providing that the banks shall cancel, in the case of cheques, bills of exchange, and promissory notes. This, of course, does not pass through any bank, and it has been regarded as a necessary safeguard to the revenue that this provision should be inserted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand that, but in addition to the means hitherto provided for cancellation you say that the person whose duty it is to cancel the stamp may use " other marks of identification."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of stamps on these proprietary medicines and patent medicines, and wines, and perfumery, the provision is the same as in the English Inland Revenue Act. This is a new provision and it is considered necessary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I see now that
it is a new provision; my attention was called to it by the fact that I did not observe it in any of the sections of the Act previously. This section gives the power to the minister to say what the value of certain commodities is; is not that a very wide power?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On proprietary and patent
medicines and perfumery, the retail price being twenty-five cents or less, the stamp tax is one cent, and as it becomes necessary that there should be some certainty in the imposition of this tax, this provision gives the minister power to determine the retail value so that the tax may be imposed in the event of any dispute arising. It is provided elsewhere in our legislation, notably in the Customs Act, that the decision of the minister shall be conclusive on certain points for the sake of uniformity and to put the question beyond controversy, and thus make the measure effectual without resorting to the courts.
It is similar to the power of valuation in customs for taxation purposes only.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Precisely, in order that
there may be a conclusive value put upon an article by the minister in any disputed case.
The price that the minister would fix would not control the price which the vendor would charge the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This power
would become operative if fraud were attempted upon the revenue. That would be the case if a medicine, which to-day sells for 25 cents or 50 cents, were to be sold at a lower price for the purpose of evading the tax.

The profits are very large in this business. In Montreal there is great competition amongst the druggists. There are cut-rate druggists. Recently I saw a certain proprietary medicine advertised as follows:

Usually sold for 25 cents; now one bottle tor 25 cents, two bottles for 26 cents.
What is the minister going to do in such
a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think the ministei would fix the price of each bottle in a case of that kind, probably at 25 cents.

Is the minister going to
