I desire to bring to the attention of the committee certain matters having relation to the 17th Battalion, Nova Scotia regiment, which left Valcartier in the month of October for the front. In making these observations I desire to place myself upon record as not having in mind any intention to make an attack upon the Minister of Militia and Defence. So far as I am personally concerned I can only say that in my judgment, in the discharge of his duties in connection with the equipping and sending to the front of a Canadian force to assist the Allies in the great conflict which is going on at the present time, he has manifested marvellous energy and very great ability. I think, however, that it is only just to the persons in Nova Scotia who are interested in the 17th Battalion, made up, as it is, of Nova Scotians, that these matters should be brought to the attention of the committee and of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, thus giving him an opportunity of stating his side of the case. Certain documents have been placed in my hands; they come from Colonel Robertson, who is in charge of this battalion. These I desire to read; they are as follows:
Valcartier Camp, Sept. 13, 1914.
The undersigned officers and non-commis. sioned officers of the Nova Scotia regimental contingents now in camp having as they believe an honest grievance on behalf of themselves,

the militia and citizens of the province of Nova Scotia, arising from treatment received from the Militia Department, desire to lay the following facts before you for your earnest consideration in the confident hope that some remedial action will be taken in their behalf.
After leaving Amherst, N.S., the officers on board the troop unanimously agreed that a request be made to have the Nova Scotians formed in a battalion under the command of the officers with the contingents. Major Robertson was asked by his senior officers to take command in event of the request being granted, and telegrams were despatched from Moncton to the Prime Minister, Colonel Hughes and Senator Dennis.
On our arrival near the camp ground on Saturday, August 22, 1914, we were obliged to find our way by inquiry to camp site. Neither rations nor tents had been provided or allotted. Owing to heavy rain on Friday night, had we not asked for leave to remain on board the train at LSvis, we would have been brought into camp in the rain and dark to forage for ourselves. No rations were issued to us until Sunday, August 23. This condition of affairs was due to headquarters having overlooked the sending of advance parties.
We were then placed in a battalion under command of an officer from New Brunswick whose character was then under investigation, and who had never shown any interest or activity in the militia. Although the Nova Scotians comprised the larger part of the provisional battalion the staff officers had been selected and the list was posted in the orderly tent No provisions had been made for a representation of any officers from Nova Scotia.
Owing to those facts Major Robertson, at the request of the Nova Scotian officers wired the Minister of Militia as follows:
" Valcartier Camp, August 23.
"Colonel the Honourable Sam. Hughes,
"On train from Quebec to Ottawa.
"Officers and men of Nova Scotian regiments comprising contingent desire to be formed into a Nova Scotian regiment commanded by Nova Scotian officers. The three officers senior to me ask me to take command. Do not wish to be merged with New Brunswick and lose identity. Consider that military qualifications and interest in militia should count. Seventy-eighth first to volunteer from Maritime Provinces. Have sacrificed all private interest for _ service and feel our request reasonable and should be granted.
"(Signed) Struan G. Robertson."
No mention of the number of men was made, it being a matter of record at Headquarters, Ottawa. The following reply was received:
" Ottawa, Ontario, August 24. "Col. Struan G. Robertson,
"Valcartier, Que.
"Please get move on and organize as suggested.
"(Sgd.) Sam. Hughes."
On or about September 1, the Camp Commandant, in the presence of all the officers commanding contingents in camp, spoke in a contemptuous maner of the move on the part of Nova Scotians for a battalion and said in effect that we had not men enough to form a battalion, thought ourselves too good to be
jointed with others, and that he would not allow us to recruit Nova Scotians from other regiments in camp or at home.
Repeated requests had previously been made for leave to recruit Nova Scotians in camp and had been refused, although the privilege had been extended to other units or they were doing so with the knowledge of the Commandant. No consideration was given the Nova Scotians, while obstacles were thrown in their way. They were not even asked to be present when the provisional battalions were made up, but tney were allotted to two separate battalions without being asked as to their wishes. With the consent of all of us an appeal was then made to the Prime Minister, but with the exception of a gracious interview on Sunday last, nothing has been done.
Two paragraphs follow to which I do not subscribe, but, in order to make the article consecutive, I will read them:
The Minister of Militia, however, by deliberate misstatements of fact, interlarded with profanity unbecoming an officer or soldier, has sought to place the province of Nova Scotia and her citizen soldiery in contempt.
On Wednesday, September 9, the Nova Scotia units were paraded before the minister and told by him, in the presence of his staff, that their officers were cowards and wire-pullers, that the province was a two-by-four province, that he would send us back to do garrison duty on our farms, and many other things unbecoming an officer.
The minister then stated that he was, as a matter of grace, going to represent Nova Scotia on the first contingent by a company in place of a battalion and would put Captain Allen in command, because John Stanfield had asked him to do so, a statement manifestly unfair to Captain Allen inasmuch as his competency and efficiency were overlooked altogether.
We can view this move on the part of the minister in no other light than that from motives of petty spite he wished to apparently honour in dishonouring Nova Scotia and break up our establishment by buying over part of our forces.
Although the units had never had an opportunity of acting as a battalion, the minister called out three senior officers to exercise the separate companies as a battalion. In a spirit of fault-finding and with intent to lower the officers in the opinion of their men he attempted to find fault with the orders given, and by doing so made a public exhibition of his own ignorance of Rattalion drill, which was apparent to even the corporals in the ranks and was detrimental to the general efficiency of the Canadian forces.	1
While we left our homes in defence of the Empire at great personal sacrifice, we do not feel that any man has a right to consign us to Hades or damn us before our time.
We hutnb'y submit that the minister and his Adjutant General are, by reason of their unfairness, partiality and proneness to use profanity, quite unfitted to organize or command forces made up of patriotic Canadians whose only desire is to serve their beloved Empire as best they can.
While we may by injustice be prevented from discharging our duty, we desire to call attention to another matter of even greater importance

in that it affects the entire force: we refer to the efficiency of the Ross rifle at present in the hands of part of the force. Some of us, having the honour to belong to the 77th and 78th Regiments which in the competitions of last year stood first and second in all Canada as rifle shots, we think we have a right to speak. In our opinion the Ross rifle is not a weapon of sufficient perfection to place in the hands of our soldiers in time of war. Among other defects we note the following:
First. The locking device of the " holt " so lacks in robustness that it is readily put out of action and renders the weapon unreliable.
Second. The magazine and loading mechanism frequently fails to function properly.
Third. The springs holding the cartridges in the magazine are inefficient; the cartridges frequently jam or are all vertically ejected.
Fourth. The mechanism whereby the cartridge shells are . withdrawn not infrequently becomes inoperative.
Fifth. The sights are inaccurate and useless over 1,200 yards.
To arm a force and send it Into battle with such a weapon is to court disaster and is criminal in the extreme. It is bur duty to make it known to you without fear or favour, knowing that our fellow soldiers from Canada may have to pay the price with their lives.
All of this we most respectfully submit for your earnest consideration.
(Sgd.) 

,
Lt.-Col. 78th Regt.
C. A. Andrews,
Lt.-Col 75.th Regt.
Struan G. Robertson, Major 78th Regt.
C. E. Bent, Captain.
L. R. Cutten, Captain.
In addition to that I have a copy of a letter from Lieut.-Col. Robertson himself which I am informed was addressed to Mr. F. B. McCurdy, M.P. It reads:
Jellalabad Barracks,
North Tidworth, 4-2-15.
F. B. McCurdy, Esq.,
Halifax, N.S.
Dear sir,-I have the unpleasant duty of reporting that the battalion known as the 17th Battalion Nova Scotians is to-day practically non-existent saving the officers, non-commissioned officers and some nineteen privates. As this condition of affairs has in my opinion been brought about by the unrelenting antagonism of the Minister of Militia to the battalion from its inception, I desire merely to lay the facts as I know them before you and allow you to judge whether or not we have reason to complain.
On organization at Valcartier, authority for which was delayed until the very last moment in defiance of Sir Robert's expressed wish, there was a scarcity of necessary equipment and stationery. There was no Oliver equipment to be had, only rifles, belts and bayonets without scabbards. They could only give us 1,000 attestation forms, while we needed upwards of 2,000, as they require to be in triplicate. No medical history sheets were available. Assignments of pay and separation cards were completed ; but, owing to a mistake in the printed
fMr. Kyte.]
form of the latter they were returned before leaving Valcartier and new forms issued for completion on the voyage.
This of course was all excusable owing to the exigencies of the case. We were promised that this would all be remedied on arrival in England.
The separation cards were sent to the pay and record office, London, on arrival in England, but were returned to us, and new cards had again to be made out and forwarded through proper channels to pay and record office, along with nominal roll of officers and men. Application was made by me repeatedly for attestation forms, but none were to be had.
On December 12, 1914, two months after our arrival, I succeeded in getting 150 forms of attestation, sufficient to attest 50 men. ' Later I got a supply sufficient to complete the battalions, but then unfortunately we had no less than 140 men in isolation on account of spinal meningitis. Medical history sheets were at length supplied us on January 14, 1915. Oliver equipment was also issued to us in January, 1915.
On arrival at -Devonport I was advised by officers on the staff that, while our discipline and appearance was excellent, Colonel Hughes had said that we were a political battalion of Sir Robert Borden's and that he had nothing to do with us and that we would never get to the front.
On arrival at Pond Farm Camp my officers and I were refused mess privileges. Harrod's manager told me that no arrangements had been made for us. By providing our own cook and waiters we were eventually given a corner of the mess room.
Repeated application for a wagon to haul supplies was made to the proper authorities and refused. Finally a wagon was borrowed and for two months it had to be used for drawing all rations and removing refuse from the lines. After sickness had broken out in our lines three wagons were given us in January, 1915.
On the removal of the 4th Brigade from Pond Farm Camp, we were kept for at least two weeks cleaning up the mess the 4th Brigade had left behind and levelling the ground. For this work we had only 9 shovels, though the establishment allows 222 shovels per battalion.
About November 20, 1914, we moved to Bustard Camp to occupy lines vacated by the Princess Patricias. Found lines in a filthy condition and only 29 tents erected for 800 men, although my orders in writing were that tents were all ready for us.
December 5, 1914, we moved to Sling Plantation. Were given only 18 huts for 800 officers and men. Huts only supposed to accommodate 30 men had to be crowded to 60. No accommodation for officers apart from their men, as in the other battalions. Result overcrowding. No officers' mess or kitchens of the men. Cooking had to be done in mud and mire, while all the other battalions of the 4th Brigade were equipped with splendid cookhouses and ranges, we were in a mud-hole. In ten days time we had 200 sick. First death from spinal meningitis December 17.
Medical officer was taken from us on Xmas day and since then we have had no qualified medical officer up to this date. With the assistance of two medical students in the battalion, four inspections a day of the huts, we came through with six deaths from meningitis and one from pneumonia.

During the whole period since our arrival in England the battalion was never once inspected by the G.O.C. or any divisional officer. We were left absolutely to our own devices. Every complaint possible was made against us and not one substantiated. Only one was investigated, and proved a complete farce.
Irf December my wife wrote me from Pictou that it was reported in Pictou I was to be sent home. On January 11, 1915, I had an interview with the G.O.C. He said that the authorities were down on me, that I had better resign, as they would get me sooner or later, that being his experience. On hearing my statement the G.O.C. said, " It is not fair of them to ask me to do this kind of thing." I declined to resign and asked for an investigation. The G.O.C. said, " there are no charges." I consulted other O.C.'s, whose advice, was not to think of resigning.
On January 22, 1915, I sent in the resignations of three of my officers who had been charged with being drunk on January If. The resignations were attached to statement of evidence taken before me. I did this solely, out of consideration for their families.
According to regulations an officer is not allowed to resign in order to escape Court Martial. The resignations were accepted, but I was relieved of my command on January 28, 1915. On Sunday, January 31 all the men of the 17th Battalion were drafted into the Highland Brigade to make good the losses from death, sickness and desertion.
My personal case is a small matter compared to the manner in which the officers and men of the battalion have been used. If a statement of our wrongs were to reach the public of Nova Scotia it would be disastrous to our party In Nova Scotia. Whether General Hughes is to blame for the discontent in the contingent or not, he certainly is blamed, as all seem to lay their grievances at his door.
The G.O.C. is a very weak man. He does not seem to understand human nature. He makes no effort to get to know the officers or men.
The contingent is certainly seething with discontent, and if the Government has any idea of extending the franchise to us, my advice would be decidedly : Don't
As for efficiency, the 120 men that we sent to the Princess Patricias are proof of that, and had we only been allowed a draft from Nova Scotia to complete the battalion to strength, we would to day have been part of the Canadian Highland instead of being a reserve battalion brigade for it without men. Our typewriter was taken from us, and I am obliged to use the pen.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Struan G. Robertson,
Lt.-Colonel.
I understand that this Colonel Struan E. Robertson is one of the officers who went oyer to Europe with the hon. Minister of Militia two years ago and was part of the rather magnificent and numerous entourage which accompanied him on that occasion. Colonel Robertson performed what I must admit was a very patriotic duty in forming a Nova Scotia regiment to be forwarded as a unit to the front to take part in the war. He was unable to complete the unit at Valcartier, and he left with 700 men. I am informed-I do not know whether the information is correct or not-that he was promised that 400 men would be forwarded to him to complete his regiment. Some weeks ago I brought this matter up in the House, my attention having been called to a certain article which had appeared in the Morning Chronicle of Halifax, signed by their special correspondent at Salisbury, Mr. Horatio C. Crowell. The right hon.'the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), stated that having received information from the acting High Commissioner in London, he was in a position to say that the charges of Mr. Crowell were absolutely untrue. The article written by Mr. Crowell in the Halifax Chronicle had reference to the treatment accorded to the Halifax regiment not only at Salisbury but at Valcartier. It was stated that the Nova Scotia regiment was disbanded, that the officers had not the privilege of the mess, that medical attendance was not available for them and that on the whole they were treated in an extremely unfair way. As a consequence the regiment broke up and a number of their men were drafted into other regiments. It is only fair to Mr. Horatio C. Crowell, the correspondent of the Halifax Chronicle, that I should put upon the records of the House the correspondence which I have just read. The correspondence emanates from Colonel Struan Robertson himself. He is a person in whom the military authorities in Canada had sufficient confidence to nominate for a very high military office when they placed him in command of the Nova Scotia regiment. If there is any misstatement of fact it is traceable to Colonel Robertson himself and certainly not to the correspondent, who satisfied himself as to the truth of the statements before he despatched them to this paper.
I stated a moment ago that Colonel Robertson was a man holding a high position in military affairs in the province of Nova Scotia. Not only that, but he is a gentleman who occupies a very high professional and social position in the county of Pictou, where he lives. He is the gentleman upon whom distinguished political honours have been-conferred by the party in office. As a Conservative he was the unanimous choice of the Conservative party in the county of Pictou in the last Dominion elections. He was the candidate who opposed my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr.Macdonald) in that election. Under all these circumstances I do think that these statements are entitled to some respect, and call foi

some explanation from the Minister of Militia. I have not brought this matter up for the purpose of reflecting in any way upon the minister, but I felt that it was only right in his interest, as well as in the interest of Colonel Struan Robertson and of the other officers who signed the protest which I have read, that an explanation should be made to the House by the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has adopted a somewhat unusual course this evening, particularly in reading to the committee and sending broadcast through the country an attack upon the general officer who is now commanding the Canadians at the front. However, he has the responsibility of that, and those who have advised him to this course, if there be any, have the responsibility of it also. I do not propose to answer the hon. gentleman in the spirit, very evident from the tone of his remarks, in which he has brought the matter to the attention of the committee. As far as he has desired to use this letter for the purpose of making an attack upon my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major General Hughes), that may be a legitimate method of party warfare if my hon. friend so considers it. He will have to take the responsibility of that also. But I have again strongly to deprecate his course in assuming to ask for information in such a manner as to cast a distinct reflection and aspersion upon the character and capacity of the general who has been selected, with the approval of Lord Kitchener, to command the Canadian division now facing the foe in the trenches.
As to the action taken with regard to Col. Struan Robertson, I regret that anything should have occurred which would lead to his being relieved of his command. I can only say that the responsibility for that rests entirely and absolutely with the War Office and with General Alderson. If my hon. friend (Mr. Kyte) desired to suggest that the authorities who are referred to in that letter mean any authorities on this side of the water, such a suggestion is absolutely without foundation. From first, to last, since our troops from all parts of Canada went across the water, we have absolutely abstained from any attempts whatever to interfere with the command or otherwise; the responsibility in regard to these men as Imperial troops has been left with the War Office and with the general in command, where it properly belongs. If the general in command did

use the language as to "other authorities," he certainly was not referring to any on this side of the water.
If the officers and men of the Nova Scotia battalion had any proper grounds of complaint of their treatment, it would seem to me that a military inquiry might have been had. I am not aware of the procedure in such cases, but I believe there is a procedure which would lead to an investigation and to the redress of any grievances, if grievances existed. I have had some correspondence on this subject, and I am at liberty to state to the House again that General Alderson and the authorities of the War Office, if they took any part in the matter, are entirely and absolutely responsible for the course which has been taken in regard to Col. Struan Robertson. The letter which has been read finds fault with the treatment of the Nova Scotians both at Valcartier and at Salisbury Plain. I have made careful inquiry as to their treatment at Salisbury Plain, and I think I have exhausted every source of information on that score. My hon. friend is mistaken in saying that I contradicted of my own knowledge anything that was said in Mr. Crowell's letter. I did not undertake to do that, because I have no personal knowledge of the matter.
Will my hon. friend pardon me? I certainly did not intend to say that; I referred to the document the right hon. gentleman received from the acting high commissioner in London.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I laid before the House the information which was forwarded to me in response to my inquiries, and since then I have had further communications on the subject, some of which 1 am prepared to bring down, although some I would prefer not to bring down for personal considerations. I do not wish unnecessarily to wound the feelings of any man in this House or outside of this House.
The treatment accorded the Nova Scotia regiment on Salisbury Plain, if my information is correct, was exactly of the same character as that accorded to the other regiments from different parts of Canada; and indeed that is not very hard to believe, because who for one moment could imagine that General Alderson or the authorities at the War Office would select a particular regiment from Nova Scotia for the purpose of discriminating against it or ill-treating it? There could be no possible motive or reason for that, and until

evidence is afforded to me to the contrary I am disposed to take the word of the authorities at the War Office, the word of the general officer commanding, the word of Col. Carleton Jones, that there was no * discrimination against these men in their treatment on Salisbury Plain.
As to the organization of the regiment at Valcartier, it was desired, and indeed hoped, that additional men might be recruited from the province of Nova Scotia which would enable the regiment to cross the Atlantic at full strength, and I discussed that with my colleague the Minister of Militia. If a little more time had been afforded before the sailing of the contingent,
I have no doubt that would have been accomplished. But the question arose at that time whether it would be better for the regiment to remain and not go forward with the contingent, thus affording them an opportunity to recruit (to full strength or whether it had better go forward on the strength it then possessed with the rest of the contingent. In discussing that with the officers, my recollection is, and I think it is absolutely correct, that the conclusion was reached that it would be better for the Nova Scotia regiment to go forward at somewhat less than strength, as they thought they would not like to be left behind when all the rest of the contingent had gone. Therefore the Nova Scotian regiment went forward as it was. As to sending forward a further contingent for that particular regiment, my hon. friend will remember, .and the House will remember, that there was a very great indisposition on the part of the War Office and the Admiralty to permit a body of armed troops to cross the Atlantic, except under special and adequate convoy. From time to time the despatch of further troops has been delayed for that and other considerations. In every case we have been governed by the representations made to us by the War Office and the Admiralty as to the times at which troops should go forward and as to the numbers in which they should go forward.
Am I to understand that the letter which my hon. friend read in the first instance was one addressed to me?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not sure,
but I will inform the House later, after making absolutely sure as to what I am about to say. I know (that one letter addressed to me and signed by several officers was withdrawn as far as some of the
officers are concerned. There may have been more than one communication to me, but I have a very large correspondence and I do not want to trust to my memory too definitely. I know that one letter of a somewhat important character which came to me, signed by some of the officers of the Nova Scotia contingent was, upon further reflection and information, withdrawn by at least one officer who had signed it in the first instance.
It seems to me that the course which my hon. friend has taken is not on the whole a very desirable course to take, for the reasons I have given. Any information of a confidential character or otherwise, with regard to this or any other regiment, will be placed before hon. members of the House who desire merely to procure information.
It is unfortunate that the Nova Scotia regiment was not recruited to full strength in the first instance. They were a very fine body of men, a very fine body of men indeed, and the disposition of the province .of Nova Scotia to send men to the front has been amply demonstrated by what has since taken place. One of the best regiments that could be seen anywhere in Canada was assembled at Halifax last December, and I had the privilege of seeing them on parade and of inspecting them. The Minister of Militia, Who saw the Halifax regiment after I had come hack, assured me that among the regiments he had seen in all parts of Canada there was certainly no better regiment than that assembled at Halifax.
Further than that, he has told me since that he knew perfectly well, from information that he had collected from different parts of the province, that if two additional regiments were desired from the province of Nova Scotia, they could be raised without any difficulty, and that they would be of a character which would compare very favourably with any regiment raised in any other part of the country. There was no disposition on the part of the Minister of Militia, so far as I observed, to discriminate in any way against the Nova Scotia regiment. Along with the Minister of Militia I met the officers of the regiment when I was at Valcartier, and I venture to say that every one of them who was present at such interview will say with me that the minister treated them in a very considerate way, and offered to do and tried to do everything that was reasonably possible under the circumstances to bring the regiment up to full strength and to have it go

forward. He left it to the option of the officers themselves as to whether the one course or the other would he pursued, and the course pursued in sending the regiment forward at less than full strength was the one which the officers themselves thought it most desirable to adopt under the circumstances.

I am not quite sure whether the right hon. gentleman was in his seat when I began my remarks. If he was present, he would not say that I had interjected anything partisan or of a party *sentiment into my remarks. I distinctly disclaim any desire to make any reflections upon the Department of Militia and Defence in this connection. This matter matter has caused considerable notoriety, not only in the province of Nova Scotia, but in other provinces of Canada. Ill addition to the communication sent by Mr. Crowell, the special correspondent of the Halifax Chronicle, communications were sent by Lieut. Frank Mynott to the Ottawa Evening Journal and the Toronto Star dealing with the same subject, so that not only the readers of the Halifax Chronicle, but the readers of those other largely-circulated newspapers had an opportunity of judging whether or not there was a substantial grievance in respect of the Halifax battalion. I regard this as a public matter in which every person is interested, and we all desire a statement from the Minister of Militia and Defence as to his responsibilities, if any, in regard to the complaint made by Colonel Eobertson. Mr. Crowell is a very respected newspaper correspondent in the province of Nova Scotia, where he has a reputation for veracity of which he is very proud, and he is entitled to have given to the House by me the authority upon which he made the complaint in the newspapers. That is my justification for the remarks that I have made.
With regard to Colonel Struan Eobertson,
I hold no brief for him. He is no friend of my political party; he is a friend of the party of the right hon. gentleman himself; and any honours, distinctions or emoluments which he has received at the hands of the people of the province of Nova Scotia have been received by him as being a supporter of the right hon. gentleman's party.

My hon. friend has enlarged upon the fact that Colonel Struan Eobertson is a Conservative in politics, and that he has been a candidate in the interest of the Conservative party. I may

say more than that, that he has been known to me for many years and that he is a personal friend of mine. I should be very sorry indeed to believe that any injustice had been done to him, either at Valcartier camp or on Salisbury Plain. The better course in such matters on the part of a military man is to follow the usual course of procedure, in case of any grievance, of making a demand for a court martial, or for an investigation. In so far as his being a Conservative or a Liberal is concerned, I would resent any injustice to Colonel Struan Eobertson if he were the strongest Liberal in the country, just as much as I would under present conditions. The question whether a man who goes out to fight for his country is a Conservative or a Liberal, in respect of any matter of this kind, weighs not one single grain in my estimation. I do not quite appreciate the motive of my hon. friend in putting forward the fact that Colonel Struan Eobertson is a Conservative. If my hon. friend desired to make a protest in this House in respect of an alleged injustice to any one of those men who happened to be a strong Liberal, I would deem it just as much my duty to take the matter up and make inquiries and have any necessary investigation as if the complaint were made in respect of a man who had 'been supporting the party to which I belong. Possibly my ihon. friend did not mean anything by stating that Col. Eobertson was a Conservative. I am quite willing to believe that such is the case. It is undesirable to attach any blame to men who are responsible for military command of our forces now facing the enemy in France until the question as to whether any fault has been committed or any grievance exists has been dealt with through the ordinary rebognized military channel. As I have already explained to my hon. friend from Eichmond (Mr. Kyte), I sent a request to the High Commissioner for Canada that the substance of those complaints should be .laid before General Alderson and before the War Office, coupled with the desire on the part of the Government of this country that, subject to ordinary military usage, which, of course, must be observed in certain matters, an investigation of the alleged grievance be made. I hope that it will be made.

In this connection, I understand that a number of the officers of the Nova Scotia regiment, who do not agree

with the views of Col. Struan Robertson, and who, according to the letter read by my bon. friend the member for Richmond, are in barracks at Tidworth, and have for some reason or other not been permitted to be attached to any of the other battalions or regiments, I understand that some of those men would like to be given an opportunity of becoming attached to some of the regiments going to France. I would ask whether something cannot be done in that regard.
I feel sure that what was done in England in regard to any of the men who went over there would be whatever was decided upon by the General Officer Commanding and by the War Office, and that fibey alone would direct anything that would be done in regard to the Nova Scotia battalion or any other battalion. I do not fancy that the military authorities in Canada would have anything to do with the direction or control of the personnel of those battalions after they reached the other side. I know some of the men of whom I speak. I have seen them in camp and I know their worth as officers and as men. Apart from any statement that Col. Struan Robertson may have made in regard to ill-treatment, those men do not share his views, and they ought not to be treated prejudicially on that account and ought to be given an opportunity of doing something.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I concur entirely in my hon. friend's appreciation of the officers whom I met at Valcartier. I thought them a fine body of men. I am no more qualified than is my hon. friend to judge of their military qualities.
Oh, oh.
Is that complimentary?	.
You are both honorary colonels.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps my
hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) and I will have to reconsider our attitude on that. However, I did have a little military experience, and I suppose my hon. friend did also, years ago. More years ago than I care to think about. I went through the military school at Halifax, then under the command of General Laurie, under the direct supervision of a good old British officer, very stem in his way, called Col. Milsom, and obtained a certificate to command and drill a company at company
drill and a battalion at battalion drill, though I am afraid that my knowledge in that regard has become a little rusty since then. But with regard to the surplus officers-because more officers went over than were actually required-the situation has not been an easy one, and I have felt a great deal of personal concern in meeting a number of them who returned from England some time in December last, and whom I had the opportunity of seeing on the train. They were, beyond question, very fine men, and I should judge very capable men, and a number of them were men of experience. They could not be provided with commands in Great Britain. The course which the War Office thought it best to pursue under the circumstances and that Gen. Alderson followed, was to return them to Canada, with' a view to their being employed in some later contingents; and I have said to the Minister of Militia that, as far as possible, consideration should be given to these men, because they had volunteered for service abroad, had been sent to Valcartier and afterwards to Great Britain, and were very earnest, their whole hearts being in their desire to serve their country.
So far as the men at Tidworth barracks are concerned, my hon. friend from Pictou will realize the difficulty of otir making suggestions with regard to the appointment of men after they have gone to the other side as Imperial troops. For example, if we should be of opinion that certain officers were very competent and capable and worthy of consideration, the authorities of the War Office or the General Officer Commanding might not concur in that opinion-it would be undesirable that any such state of affairs should be brought about. Subject to that consideration, the importance of which the hon. member for Pictou, I am sure, will be the first to recognize, I should be very glad, and I am
9 p.m. sure the Minister of Militia would be very glad, to assist in any possible and proper way to carry out the suggestions which the hon. gentleman has made. If my hon. friend would send me a memorandum giving the names of the officers, I should be glad to confer with the Minister of Militia with regard to the matter, to see if anything can properly be done to meet the suggestion. It would be my most earnest wish that something could be done.

I am advised that
these officers of the Nova Scotia regiment, who are in barracks at Tidworth, occupy an

altogether different position from those officers who returned about the beginning of the year from Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They went over with commands-the hon. gentleman means that they differ in that respect?

Yes, and differ in
their status, as their services are not being dispensed with. They simply remain there occupying positions as supernumeraries. It is not suggested that they come back. I should be glad to communicate to the right hon. gentleman the names of some of these officers whom I know, with a view to having the matter dealt with. 1 do not think the right hon. gentleman should blame the hon. member for Richmond for calling the attention of the House to this question, for I think he had a perfect right to do it.

With the
motives of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) I have nothing to do. With the remarks he has made and the contents of the letter he has read I have to do. He is correct in stating that a year ago Major Struan Robertson accompanied me through the fields of Europe and saw the various manoeuvres, which would show to an ordinary observer that I could not have a very vindictive feeling towards that gentleman. The fact that Major Struan Robertson wired me on the way up with the Nova Scotians that they were coming in strength and asking to be formed into a Nova Scotia regiment with himself, Major Struan Robertson as Lt.-Golonel, was cheering to me, especially when followed up with telegrams from the same gentleman and from other distinguished gentlemen from the province of Nova Scotia, stating that they had fifteen hundred men from that province coming to Valcartier and asking that we should recognize them as a Nova Scotia regiment. Nothing gave, me greater pleasure than to wire back that I would constitute them a Nova Scotia regiment. On their arrival m camp it transpired that they had less than half a thousand men, not quite enough for half a battalion. I saw Major Robertson and discussed the situation with him and asked him what he proposed doing-should we recruit more men from Nova Scotia? He said that what was meant by the statement that they had fifteen hundred men from Nova Scotia was that, considering the number of men they had brought direct ik'om the province, together with the number of those in the battalion from other

parts of Canada, they could recruit a regiment upwards of a thousand strong. To tihis proposition I personally made no objection. I pointed out, however, that many of these men had lived for years in the West and had made their homes there, and that there was an attractiveness about the prairie life and the mountain life, and I warned him that he would find difficulty in winning these men away from the corps to which, they belonged. I told him that if he attempted to win men away from these corps from the West he must do it with the consent of the officers of the corps. I think that was only honourable. As a matter of fact, while there were a very large number of men in other corps who came from Nova Scotia they preferred remaining with their comrades with whom they had come to Valcartier rather than leave and join the Nova Scotia battalion under Major Struan Robertson. The next proposition he made to me was to recruit up at home; but that was deemed impossible within the time at our command. I need not enter into the detans of the hurry of getting troops away by the 1st of October, but it was regarded as impossible to carry out that recruiting, especially as not only from the troops in camp but also from the reports that were coming from the militia in Nova Scotia, it was found that Major Struan Robertson was not regarded as the. best leader of men from that province.
At the last moment we permitted Major Robertson to recruit men from Toronto, from the Maritime Provinces, or from any part of the country in which he could get them, and in that way he increased the strength of his regiment up to 650 or 700 men.
Let me say here that a more athletic, bright-eyed or soldierly looking lot of fellows than the Nova Scotians could not be picked up anywhere under the sun. We recognized that; they knew it without our recognizing it. An arrangement seemed to have been entered into, however, by two or three of the senior officers, without consultation with the company officers or with the men, that they should form a little close corporation of their own, and tolerate nothing which would not have the effect of keeping these men at its head. The proposal that the regiment should remain behind, enlist to full strength and go across the water later, was not received with favour. Many of the officers and men expressed the view that if this suggestion were carried out they would be looked upon as

dodging the issue, shirking their work, or showing the white feather; and these were qualities which they did not wish to have attributed to them or to their province. That proposal was, therefore, rejected. Perhaps before mentioning this phase of the matter I should have referred to the fact that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick had each half a battalion of home men. It was proposed that there should be a Maritime Province battalion similar to the one the formation of which was recently started but not completed, the idea being changed to that of giving each province a battalion for the third contingent. The proposition to have a Maritime Province battalion, while acceptable to a great number of officers and men, was indignantly rejected by Major Struan Robertson and the two officers who were associated with him. The reason was evident. Colonel McLeod, being the senior officer, would take command of the regiment and these other gentlemen would be relegated to subordinate positions. That proposition, therefore, also fell through. Week in and week out, until the week before the troops sailed, I did my level best to bring about a happy solution of this Nova Scotia difficulty, but any suggestion, the carrying out of which would not keep Major Struan Robertson in command, and the officers associated with him in second and third positions, was rejected. I made the suggestion that, as it was desired that Nova Scotia should be definitely represented in the first contingent, one composite or individual company-that splendid company from the town of Truro, for instance-should be sent as representing the province, and that the others should remain at home and recruit to full strength. That proposal was also rejected; therefore the regiment had to be allowed to sail. The regiment was gazetted, Major Robertson was put in orders as Lieutenant-Colonel commanding, with Colonel Cameron as second in command and Colonel Andrews as junior major. The regiment sailed, and from that hour up to the present I have neither directly nor indirectly had anything to do with the matter. I have received scores of letters from officers and men complaining of the treatment	accorded them; I have never
answered these letters. I did send a cable in answer to Captain Allen, declining to receive any communications from him, and advising him that the commanding officer, General Alderson, was the proper person
to whom to send any complaints or any communications upon matters affecting the regiment. I did not interfere with the regiment, either directly or indirectly, when the accountant and paymaster general of the Militia Department was asked why the returns from the regiment came in so late. He communicated the definite reply from Colonel Ward, paymaster of the regiment in England, that Colonel Ward had tried to get from the Nova Scotia regiment the commanding officer's attestation papers, but that up to the middle of December he had failed to do so. He commented in very strong terms upon the incapacity of this officer. However, I have had nothing to say in the matter; for various reasons I declined to interfere.	-
Reference has been made in the communications which have been read to the committee as to my having made some re: marks to the regiment. I would like to have had those remarks reported. I admit frankly that I did not compliment the three officers who had, in these and other cases, prevented the formation of the regiment in such manner as to reflect credit upon the service. But the men, as I said then and say now, were in every respect a credit to the province of Nova Scotia, in conduct, in drill, in rifle shooting, in soldiery bearing, in all that goes to make up a good soldier.
Twelve regiments were selected for the front from Salisbury Plain. A division is made up of twelve regiments, and it was known before the troops left Canada that several regiments would have to remain behind when the troops went to the front. When the division was formed at Salisbury, five regiments were left behind. One of these has been formed into a cavalry regiment; four regiments, therefore, of the original lot of 33,000 men, are still in England, and will from time to time make up losses in the regiments at the front. Unfortunately, casualties are occurring from day to day; these men will in turn, be drafted over to take the places of those who have suffered casualties. A number of the Nova Scotia boys have already gone to the front and are doing splendid service with the Princess Patricia regiment. I understand that some of the officers also have been taken. I have every faith in the Canadian officers in command of the troops, and I have sufficient confidence in the British officers to be able to say that no injustice would
143?

be done to any Canadian regiment. The units of the Canadian forces are all treated as being on an absolutely equal footing.

I was inclined to think, when I first read it, that the publication if the article by Mr. Crowell was a mistake but I did not know at that time that he had so much evidence to justify his statements. It seems to me that while it is not wise to ventilate these military matters too much while the war is in progress, there is sufficient evidence before the minister to require a full and clear explanation, not only on the part of the officers and the men who have gone to the front in this battalion from Nova Scotia, but also on the part of the numerous relatives of these officers and men in that province who are very much disturbed over the statements that have been made in the press. I think it is due to the minister that these matters should be cleared up and that the truth should be given to the public, who are so deeply interested. It appears that at the time -Mr. Crowell wrote the letter for the Morning Chronicle he had ample evidence before him. The letter that was addressed to the Prime Minister contained the statements that are made in Mr. Crowell's letter. The other letter addressed to the hon. member for Queens-Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) contains the same statements, and they must have been in the possession of members of the Government now for some time. A memorandum has been placed in my hands which gives some further proof corroborating the statements of Colonel Struan Robertson and the other two or three officers who signed that document. A large number of other parties, many of whom are now in Canada, and no doubt could be produced as witnesses, have corroborated what Colonel Struan Robertson said, and what was published in the Morning Chronicle. Let me read this memorandum:
We, the undersigned officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 17th Nova Scotia . Battalion, having- read the article published in the Morning Chronicle of Pebraury 25, 1915, signed by H. C. It appears that Colonel Robertson was permitted to recruit men from other parts of Canada, as the minister has stated, and he did recruit a number of men. I presume the men who have signed this memorandum were among those recruited into the Nova Scotia regiment from other parts of Canada. I do not feel satisfied with the minister's explanation. Are we to believe that the statements that are made by Colonel Struan Robertson in regard to the minister's own conduct at Valcartier are all true and must be accepted by the country? If they are true it is an extraordinary position that the minister has taken. Why, let me ask, did the minister take such a position in regard to the soldiers who were sent from that province to fight for the Empire? I am not complaining as to what took place at Salisbury Plain because the officers responsible at Salisbury are not here and are not represented here. I have not a word to say about what was done at Salisbury Plain; but I think it is due to the House and to the country that the minister should give a better explanation than he has as to what took place at Valcartier. It is stated in the letter read by the hon. member for Richmond that on the 9th of November the Nova Scotia regiment was paraded before the minister, and that the minister said, in the presence of his staff of officers, that the Nova Scotia officers were cowards and wire-pullers, and that Nova Scotia was a two-by-four- province anyway. I can hardly believe that a man occupying the position of Minister of Militia would so far forget himself as to make statements like that in the presence

of officers of other battalions. How could he expect these officers of the Nova Scotia regiment to respect him or to serve him as the head of our forces if he used such language as that to them in the presence of other officers? I think the language is very unbecoming, and I do not think the minister has at all justified himself in regard to that matter. What right had he to say that they were cowards before they had had an opportunity to show their courage? At that time they were simply in camp at Valcartier. How can he tell whether a man is a coward or not? I want to tell him that the men sent from Nova Scotia are not cowards, and also that Nova Scotia is not a two-by-four province.

Did any of
these men refuse to go with the first contingent? They wanted to go, not like his breed.

Then, why call them
cowards, that the minister had no right to say to any soldier who offered his services to the Empire at a time like this and prior to his having a chance to show his mettle on the battlefield that he is a coward, and I resent such an expression on behalf of the officers of the 17th Regiment. I do not wish it to pass without giving my views on it. I do not know what right the minister has to say that Nova Scotia is a two-by-four province. I want to tell him that the smallest man in Nova Scotia is not afraid of him, and that he would not be afraid to attempt to knock the stuffing out of him if he got a chance. He might not be able to do it, but he would try; and if he did knock the stuffing out of him, if we are to judge by his appearance here to. night and the- exhibition he has made of himself in this matter, there would not be much left.
There seems to have been ample proof in the hands of Mr. Crowell at the time he published the article in question that he had a perfect right to publish it and that it was his duty to do so. I think it is extraordinary. I expected the minister to give us some explanation; I did not expect him to allow such statements to go on record without either explaining them in some way or giving some reason for his extraordinary conduct. It appears that he admits the statements were correct-that he did call the officers of the 17th cowards in the presence of his other officers and spoke disrespectfully of the whole province of Nova Scotia; and I want the people of
Nova Scotia to know what the minister has to say about them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I regret that my hon. friend has found it necessary to procure and read in the House statements reflecting upon the treatment of Canadians by the authorities of the War Office. 1 do not understand what his motive can be unless he desires to inspire in the people of Canada a distrust in the Imperial authorities at this juncture in our affairs. If that is his motive-and I do not know of any other motive that he could have had in procuring the statements and reading them to the House-then I say it is a motive which does no credit to him under present conditions.
It is generally well known that no one in this House, either on this side or the other side, pays much attention to anything the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) says.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Order.
Does'the hon. gentleman dispute it?
Yes, it is disputed.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) must not put words into my mouth. I distinctly denied having made any such speech, but he cannot draw me into any dispute over the matter contained in that letter. The letter carries on its face its own condemnation. The hon. gentleman is good at boasting of his bravery. He is not at the front; he has never volunteered for this or any other service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is well
known that in this country, as well as in the Mother Country, the military power is subject to the civil power. Military men, like men in civil life, are not infallible. My hon. friend brought to the attention of the committee information which he has had that certain language had been used by the Minister of Militia on a certain occasion. If the Minister of Militia had used such language everybody must admit that he would have been greatly in the wrong. The minister repudiated it. He says that he has not used such language, and we have to accept his word.	-

The minister
repudiated it before the hon. member for Guysborough spoke.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He brought
this to the attention of the House and gave the minister an opportunity of repudiating it. My hon. friend now states that he did not use the language. If the minister states that he did not use such language, that is enough for everybody.
It should have been, but it was not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend says that he did not do it, and we must accept his statement, but we say that if he had done it he would have been greatly in the wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I might add to what my hon. friend the Minister of Militia has said that when this letter, which has been read in the House, came to my attention it contained some statements attributing to the Minister of Militia language of that kind in regard to the officers in question and in regard to the province of Nova Scotia. I brought the matter to his attention, and he most indignantly denied to me that he had ever used any language of the kind.

I might say- not that I care a snap of the finger for the whole matter-that one of the officers who signed it did so because he was asked to do so. I have a declaration-I did not think it worth while to bring it to the House -stating that the whole thing was a tissue of falsehoods and that he was asked to sign it in order to get a set of flags for the regiment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Militia must not snap his fingers so easily as that. My hon. friend can lose his temper, and I think that is what has happened to him. The atmosphere has been thick with the rumours and reports of strong language used at Valcartier. They may be true or they may not be, and if the hon. gentleman says that this is not true we must accept his word. So far the incident is at an end, but it is right that upon the floor of Parliament the minister should repudiate having used any such language if he has not done so. It is better for himself, and it is in the interest of his department that he should have an opportunity of setting the matter right as soon as it could be set right.

The right hon. the leader of the Opposition must remember that I am not finding the slightest fault

with the hon. member for bringing the letter up. The only thing I find fault with is that an hon. member, who does not happen to be a military man, should read a letter in this House casting an aspersion upon General Alderson. Without a vestige of proof as to the truth of the statements contained in the letter, the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair), with characteristic fairness, tried to make a political attack.

I listened very carefully to the hon. gentleman speaking in the first instance. I expected he would deny the statement in the letter read by the hon. member for Richmond. But I feel quite certain that if he examines Hansard he will find that he did not deny it, and my reason for putting it so plainly to him was that he had not denied it. I am quite certain that he made no denial. He admitted that he had used very strong language .and he admitted also that he had not complimented the officers. I referred to it only because the hon. gentleman had failed to deny it in his speech, but if he says now that he did not make these statements I must accept his denial. ,
I said that I spoke in strong terms of the conduct of three officers-
Why?
-but that I spoke in the highest praise of the rest of the officers and men. That was in my first statement. That would have been shown to be the fact had my language on that occasion been reported.
I would like to know why the minister spoke in strong terms of those officers. What reason had he to speak in strong terms of the officers of this regiment? If there is a reason let us have it.
What do you call strong terms?

I would like to ask the minister a question. I do not want to ask him anything that I ought not to ask in his capacity as a military officer. Would he give the committee the status of the 12th battalion ?
That is one of the details of the brigade which was left at Salisbury.

Why was the New Brunswick battalion as well as the Nova Scotia battalion left behind? Probably he may say that this is a matter for the officers at

Salisbury Plain to decide. But if the minister has any information I can assure him that the people in New Brunswick would like to know the reason why. There has been a great deal of adverse comment in New Brunswick on account of it, along the same lines as the comment respecting the 17th. We never heard that the regiment, asv a regiment, had been treated unfairly, but there is a great deal of wonder and comment in New Brunswick as to why this regiment, which certainly contained as good material as would be found in any part of Canada, had been left in England while practically all the rest of the force had gone across the water. We know that certain other corps forwarded from New Brunswick the engineer corps, for instance, were taken across and have been at the front because we are receiving letters from the boys and we know where they are and what they are doing.

The artillery
too.

The artillery were taken across, and there are a lot of good men in that corps. But it is a remarkable fact that the infantry regiment have been left in England. It looks as though there had been something like discrimination and that is why I think the minister should take us into his confidence, and tell us the reason why the infantry battalion were passed over or treated so differently from the engineer and artillery corps.

I have no explanation whatever. We had nothing whatever to do with picking the regiments that were left at home. They are all good, all magnifieient riflemen. There is no New Brunswick regiment, I may inform my hon. friend there are a lot of splendid fellows from New Brunswick, and they are allied with the boys from Quebec, the British and French stock from Quebec, and they constitute one of the best regiments in the service. The only thing that can be suggested is that Colonel McLeod was taken ill with pneumonia; he was laid up for some time, and therefore was not able to keep in touch with matters. We have had nothing to do with the question as to which regiments should be taken and which left.

There are other officers besides Colonel McLeod. I do not know that I would be doing myself justice if I did not state that the gentleman, who I understand, is second in command, Major Guthrie, is just as good 91
an officer as Colonel McLeod. Perhaps I may be pardoned for saying that there are a good many people in New Brunswick who have just as much confidence in his military ability as they have in the military ability of Colonel McLeod. It does not seem that the temporary illness of Colonel McLeod ought to be sufficient excuse for these men remaining where they, were. Is Colonel McLeod still in command of the regiment?	[DOT]Major-General HUGHES:	I understand
so; I have heard nothing to the contrary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is naturally a good deal of impatience and regret among all the regiments which have been assigned to duty in England, that they were not allowed to go to the front at once. We have reason to know that, and it is greatly to the credit of the officers and men that they should have so keen a desire to proceed to the front and engage in active service. Assuming, as we are bound to assume, that the efficiency of all these regiments is practically the same, my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) will remember that it was absolutely necessary that some should remain in Great Britain, whose services would be utilized in the way the Minister of Militia has described. I took the responsibility at the Valcartier camp of deciding that all the forces there assembled should go forward, and I took that course for the reason that they were assembled; that they were all ready, and that they were all keen to go. There was no arrangement made in Canada as to which should go to the front first, and. it was believed at that time that our men would go to the front much earlier than actually happened. We knew from the information afforded to us by the War Office that very large reinforcements might be required in the immediate future, and as the men were assembled there, and as .transports and convoys for a large fleet of transports could be secured, it seemed best that they should all go forward to Great Britain, complete their training, and be available in the immediate future to furnish reinforcements which could reach the front within five or six days. It was with that idea, after consultation between the Minister of Militia and my colleagues and myself that the whole force went forward. When the troops arrived in England, they did not go to the front at once, and naturally those who did not form part of the division when it did proceed were greatly disappointed. I am sure the people of this country will realize



that it is absolutely no reflection on those who remained behind that at the moment they did not go forward with their comrades, but I think they can have the assurance that at the first possible opportunity the War Office will avail itself of their services.
The Prime Minister makes a very plausible apology for the Minister of Militia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was not
apologizing.

If I should ask for any information which the Minister of Militia or the Prime Minister does not care to give to the House, I will have no fault to find with them for refusing it. As I understand it, these regiments which are left behind in England will cease to exist as battalions, and I believe the 12th and 17fih have already ceased to exist as such. Then, as I understand it also, when these men go forward they will not go forward as battalions, but simply as drafts to fill up vacancies in other battalions. Am I right in understanding that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These are all matters that must be determined by the authorities at the War Office and by the General Officer Commanding, so that it is useless and undesirable for us to attempt to decide them here. As my hon. friend, who I understand is a military man-
I am not.
He is a colonel.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not even an honorary colonel?
Not even honorary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then he is not in the same class as my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and myself.
There has been a great discrimination in that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Prompt steps should be taken to remedy a discrimination of that kind. Our overseas forces are under the direction of the War Office. They were enlisted as Imperial troops, and-the direction of them must remain with the War Office.

I suppose that is all the information the ministers feel like giving,

and I do not wish to ask for more than they are willing to volunteer. Let me ask as to the status of some 150 or 160 officers who went over with the contingent without being attached to any particular corps, and some of whom have returned. I understood the Prime Minister to say that it was on his recommendation that these officers were allowed to go forward. I know that some of them have returned and I know that some have not, because there were three officers from my own neighbourhood who were included in the number, and two have come hack and one has not. Is anything being done to find places for these gentlemen?

Of course, the hon. gentleman refers now to the officers who have returned and who are capable officers and who are recommended. We are finding places for them as rapidly as we can. A great many of them have already been placed and we are doing our best to place them here, either as instructors or in the third contingent. Those who have remained in England are also being utilized to the best advantage. A number of them have taken service with British regiments, some have beejj drafted into other regiments, some went with the Patricias, and I am sorry to say that the casualty lists from day to day show that these details will not have long to wait before they will be in the firing line at the front. Some of the officers who have returned naturally feel aggrieved at not getting positions, but we are utilizing every man in some capacity or another. We do not know the exact number who are not yet employed, but they are very few.
Have all these officers been provided with pay and subsistence? .
They are all under pay.

I wish to ask the Minister of Militia if Dr. Mignault, of Montreal, and some of the officers of the 65th regiment have asked permission to organize a Freneh-Ganadian contingent, ahd if so why did be refuse their request?

I have great pleasure in correcting my hon. friend. There was an offer on behalf of a number of French-Canadian gentlemen for an hospital corps which we transmitted to the War Office which has charge of all these matters. The War Office cheerfully granted that request, and the corps is now formed. I da

not know who is at the head of it, but it is entrusted to the distinguished gentlemen of French-Canadian nationality, who are connected with the medical profession in Montreal. That hospital corps will soon be organized and ready for the front. As far as the French Canadian regiment is concerned, Dr. Mignault was active in organizing it; but like an old war-horse, he fell back to his old profession and went into the medical service instead of into the combatant service. He has done splendid work in organizing the 22nd Regiment, and he has already done splendid work in organizing a hospital corps, giving of his time and of his money.

When he, with some military men from Montreal, came on a deputation last fall to see the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia, did not that deputation ask permission to form a French Canadian contingent?
I think so, and we gave them permission and they formed a splendid regiment. It is under Colonel Paquet at Amherst.
Was not permission given to form only a regiment?

That was all
that was asked for.
Did not they ask permission to organize a brigade?

I have no recollection of their asking permission to organize a brigade. They would have to organize a regiment, because a brigade is composed of regiments. Our French-Canadian fellow-countrymen gave splendid service in the first contingent. The Maritime Provinces Regiment, the Quebec Corps, the Montreal Corps, the Northwest Corps and some of the Ontario Corps have a number of our French Canadian fellow-countrymen with them giving good service. Colonel Meighen speaks in high terms of them. Colonel Farquhar spoke in the highest terms of Lieutenant Papineau. Those who have written home from the front all speak in the highest terms of the French-Canadian boys. We have the 22nd Regiment; we have another regiment organized under Colonel Archambault, who was given command some days ago. Colonel Paquet is going to form another one. It will only be a few days until it is formed. That will make three regiments composed solely of
French-Canadians. I venture to predict that they will do splendid service at the front.

I am very glad to hear the minister make that statement, because there has been a campaign carried on in certain portions of Canada for the last six months alleging that the French-Canadians have not done their duty in this war.
And the Eng-lishGanadians too.

I have heard it dozens of times. I have read it in the newspapers in the Maritime Provinces friendly to the Government, and it has been the one unpleasant aspect of the discussion of this war in the public press of Canada. In the first place I am glad that the hon. minister makes that statement, and in the second place I congratulate him very highly for having the manhood to stand up and tell the exact truth. I hope that when this war is over, we shall hear no more in Canada about the French-Canadians not having done their duty.

There has been all sorts of tittle-tattle, but we do not pay any attention to it. There are some who say that the British-Canadians have not done their duty. Some of the first regiments which went forward were chiefly made up of British-born men who had settled in the West, but they were practially Canadians, having lived in this country for five or six years or more. I can point to many French-Canadians and British-Canadians who have done splendid service. I just want to say that there is nothing whatever in the stories that have been sent out. Every Canadian whether British or French, has done his duty splendidly.

1 would like to point out to the hon. member for Carleton that it is iquite usual for persons to criticize, perhaps not too wisely, persons engaged in military matters. I recall to mind a verv distinguished officer who was very roundly censured and was referred to in this Rouse as an Englishman by the name of French; but it did not hurt his reputation or injure his status at all in the British army or in the opinion of his countrymen.

I am glad that the facts have been elicited, and that the hon. minister has acknowledged that the French-Canadians have done their duty as well as those of other nationalities have done. I can corroborate what my hon. friend the member for Carleton has just said. I have

read in many English newspapers in this country allegations that the French-tCana-dians have been very remiss in enlisting and in doing their duty towards the Empire. The other day the Saturday Post, of Winnipeg, cast a reproach upon the FrenchjCanadians for not enlisting. What I did not like last fall was that the minister was too lax in acknowledging the fact that the French Canadians had enlisted in large numbers. The first time that he admitted the fact was when a deputation from Montreal, composed of Dr. Mignault and some of the officers of the 65th regiment, came here to ask permission to organize a brigade. Before that, some important newspapers like the Evening News of Montreal had stated that very few French Canadians had enlisted. That was done for a purpose. There was talk of an election at that time, and reflections were cast on my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Endeavours were made to create the impression throughout the country that the French-Canadians were not loyal, and that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition could not be trusted to form a Government while the Empire was at war. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence had a knowledge of the facts all that time, and he never admitted them until he. was forced to do so when the deputation came here.

I am somewhat obliged to my hon. friend the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) for referring to a remark which I made in the House a year ago. Fortunately I have before me every word that I said. I am going to read it now to the .House, and I hope that my hon. friend will be daring enough to go back to his newspapers and ask them if they will publish every word instead of the garbled reports w'hich they have been publishing throughout this country for the last six months. Perhaps my hon. friend the minister does not know it, but in one of the campaign sheets which his friends sent out as far back as November last, was a report of the statement that I made in the House on the first day of June. I oast no reflections whatever upon the honour, ability or integrity of Field-Marshal Sir John French. I was discussing in this House on the first day of June last the general staff of the minister, and I had discuss-ed it in this House before; and the general staff that is in existence now was not the product nor the result of the conduct of the present minister. I condemned it before he became minister,

and I have condemned it since, and I condemn it now. I am not going into any discussion of if; but I think, if I wanted any justification for my remarks a year ago, the results of the last six months have amply justified my opinion. That, however, is a matter which we may discuss later on in this debate. For the benefit of my hon. friend from Annapolis, I will read what I said about Sir John French. My hon. friend will find my remarks on page 4620 of the Revised Hansard under date of June 1, 1914. I sent out 'a few moments ago for the unrevised Hansard, but .1 was told that the distribution office did not have it. I can assure my hon. friend that there has not been an " i " dotted nr a " t " crossed between the unrevised and the revised. This is what I said about Sir John French:
I am glad to hear the minister admit that he can get along with a smaller engineer service corps, although he refers only to the regular corps and not to the militia.
In my humble judgment he could get along without a whole lot of militia engineer companies that he has at present. The principal cause of the trouble with the minister and his top-heavy militia is the report of a general by the name of French, who came to this country some years ago, and in my judgment his visit was one of the greatest misfortunes that has befallen Canada.
Some hon. MEMBERS :	Hear, hear !

Just at this point my
friend's friends all over Canada stop. They have not given the rest of what I said, but L am going to give it now. I know my friend from Annapolis is the last man who would have the manhood to get up in his constituency and repeat what I stv about to read.

Order.
MrT5 CARVELL:	No "Order" abotn it.
He deserves this. (Reading):
General French may be all right from the English standpoint. He is a general of distinction, but he is a man who has been educated entirely along different lines from those which thje conditions in Canada present. His life has been spent soldering, he is a born soldier:
Do hon. gentlemen opposite find any fault with that? Do they send that out in their campaign literature? Not by any means. (Reading):
.-he does not believe a man has any business working on a farm or in a factory or anywhere else, except a few who should work in order to make money to keep the soldiers. If you had half the people in the Empire in the army you would not have enough to satisfy General French. I told the late Minister of Militia publicly and privately that in adopting the ridiculous and unreasonable report made by this

gentleman, he had committed a great mistake. It might be all right if General French was reporting on the conditions in Bulgaria, or Russia, or Germany, or even in Italy, hut when ' it comes to a country like Canada where there is not a possibility of trouble, his ideas are ridiculous* There is .no more possibility of a war breaking out between Canada and any country in the world than there is of the Minister of Militia or myself committing suicide between now and tomorrow morning.

Oh, oh.
Mr. CARVELL.:	Let my friends just
have patience. The trouble is they have not read what I stated. (Reading):
There might, of course, be a possibility of the Empire being at war and we might find it our duty to volunteer, as in the case of the war in South Africa.
The Empire war has come. And we have volunteered.
