And I want to tell my hon. friend from Annapolis that within a fortnight after the war broke out I personally went to the Minister of Militia and volunteered my services as an officer, and told him that if he would allow me I would raise a battery of artillery and would take it. I went back to him before Christmas and repeated my request. I wonder if my friend from Annapolis has done as well as that. Why, he would run so that you could not see his heels for dust. Talk about the man from Annapolis volunteering to fight anything! The idea is preposterous. No wonder he grins like a Cheshire cat over there. I hope he will have the manhood to go back to his constituency and read what I say here tonight, and read also what I said on the 1st of June last. Then I want him to be man enough to offer his services or try to do some little thing to maintain this Empire in this great war, and not come here and be small enough to throw mud at the men who have tried to do something for the Empire's 'cause.

I desire to ask the Minister of Militia a question for information with regard to the enlisting of French-Canadians. I understand that in the first contingent there was a very large proportion of French-Canadians. What was the number?
We have never made up the statement on the lines of nationality.

I understand there were
fully 2,500.
I do not know. We have not taken the figures that way.

I understood that three
regiments were being x'ecruited. How many would that represent.

That would
mean 3,000 men besides those
10 p.m. who went in the first contingent, or with the various artillery corps, the medical corps, the army service corps-oh, they have done splendidly.
There were many French-Canadians from New Brunswick and a lot from the Northwest.

Not that I am impressed by the sympathy of my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), but I have always been proud of my fellow-countrymen, the French-Canadians, especially since the outbreak of this war. They knew that. I have said behind the scenes what I state openly, that I am proud of the splendid way our men have come forward. For the first contingent the country boys all over had no opportunity to enlist, for it was raised very rapidly; the news hardly reached the remote settlements before the regiments were full. I passed a French-Canadian station between here and Val-cartier and saw on the platform a lot of fine young men. I asked if any of their men had gone to the front. They said: " No, we can't go." "Why?" '"No men are being taken from here." I said: " All you have to do is to enlist." But they did not know how to enlist. I had the matter brought to the attention of the officers, and inside of a week fourteen of those boys joined the corps. There was a splendid response wherever the boys had an opportunity. The same was true of Ontario among the English-speaking population. But they had really no opportunity to get into the first contingent.

I take it that, from what the minister has said, allowing for the number who volunteered in the first contingent, the French Canadian regiments that are being formed, the men enlisting in the Maritime Provinces and the West, and the men who went with the medical corps and other bodies, close upon 10,000 French-Canadians must have enlisted for this war.
I could not give the figures, but there are 3,000 infantry men and 4,000 or 5,000 others and probably more.

I make this remark in justice to the men who have enlisted and to the province of Quebec. Many things

!
appear in the French Canadian press which are not read in the other provinces. Our people read the press of the other provinces, but unfortunately the people of other provinces do not read the French Canadian press of Quebec. They do not get the information which they ought to have. Last night I congratulated the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) upon the contributions from Port Colborne, in his constituency. But the remarkable fact is that the province of Quebec has contributed $1,450,000 to the Patriotic Fund, while Ontario, with a population of about a million greater, has contributed only $1,200,000. Taking into account the population and resources of the people, I think Quebec has done magnificently.

Can the hon. gentleman tell us what proportion was contributed by Montreal and what by the rest of
the province?
I cannot; Montreal is included as a part of the province of Quebec.
Yes, but the financial institutions there contributed a considerable proportion.
I thought the hon. gentleman would be glad to know that Quebec had made so good a showing in such a patriotic way.

I desire to make a few remarks in comment upon the very characteristic utterance of the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell.) I made what I supposed was an innocent remark and was somewhat surprised to find that it met with such a vivid retort; though, knowing his disposition, I suppose I ought not to have been surprised. The hon. gentleman made a very great display of courage. I do not know that I could object very much to that if he had not seen fit to institute a very unfavourable comparison between himself and myself in that regard. I do not pretend to be anything of a lion, but I do with the greatest emphasis assert that I object very much to having it understood that I have not ' as much courage as the hon. member for Carleton. I do not pretend to be brave or warlike, but when it comes down to	hard	courage Ithink	I possess	quite	as much
of that commodity as my hon. friend. He asserted that he was very anxious to act as an officer when this war broke out; that he offered his valuable services in that

capacity, and that they were not accepted. I am not surprised that his services were not accepted. A gentleman w(ho would say that the well-considered report of the man who is in command of the British forces is nonsense, a man who would criticize Field Marshal French in the terms which he read to the committee tonight, would, I think hardly be a fit and proper person to serve under this commander. If my hon. friend were to enlist, I am afraid there would be a movement on fjoot among his friends to have him supersede Field-Marshal French. If my hon. friend had been animated with so much patriotism; if that courage, an exhibition of which we had to-night, did so consume him, he would have had an opportunity,. I am certain, of serving his country; he might have gone into ithe trenches, in a capacity which would be more commensurate with his ability; a place where he might do some good. My hon. friend objected to my reference to his speech. I 'do not see that anything that he read from Hansard established the fact that my reference was unfair; I think he even made a bad matter worse. I noticed, however, that certain remarks that he did make in the course of his speech, he did not read to the committee. My hon. friend last year was incensed with, a great horror of war, a great, objection to things military. Anything in the shape of a soldier was very offensive to him. Referring to the brave men who today are at the front fighting our battles, he used these words: " The men there are dudes, lying around and drinking booze." He attacked Field-Marshal French; he said his report was worthless. He referred to him in what I regard as an insolent manner: "an Englishman by the name of French." He attacked members of our militia, and, not satisfied with that, he proceeded to attack even the good old Fenian raid veterans of Nova Scotia, charging that they were perjurers and that sort of thing. But now my hon. friend, who so despised anything military last year, comes forward before his leader and goes through this by-play of offering to act as an officer, when he knows that he would not be accepted. My hon. friend to-night assumed the roar of a lion, but concealed merely the bray of the jackass.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
After these two
speeches 1 think it is my duty to remind the committee that the item under consideration is $174,000 for salaries.

I think it is as well, after the speech that we have just had, that, lest the attention of the country be called away from it, emphasis should be laid upon the fact that in this country no distinctions of nationality are drawn as between the different classes of men who are volunteering for service. There is a higher and broader standpoint from which to look upon this matter than that of any little political capital that may he made, one way or the other. There is no difference of opinion between our nationalities in this country as to what our duty is and as to our willingness to perform that duty. I think what has been said to-night will stop any talk along that line. Tt was with regret that I had these things said to me in the course of private conversation; on such occasions I have endeavoured always to straighten them out and to point out that these things might be considered in a light which would be absolutely unfair to portions of the community. Some people forget that to the Canadian boy war was a new thing; the situation in which we were placed was so new to him that he was not, for the moment, seized of his duty. Our friends who came to us from the old land were reared in a different school. Immediately upon hearing the sound of the alarm, they understood its meaning, and many of them enlisted at once. As soon, however, as the Canadian-born boy's duty was impressed upon him, no matter what his parentage, he rose to the occasion and is now ready to do his full duty just as well as the British-born subject does his.

I have never brought these questions up; frankly, I have always dodged them, as I believe that it is in the public interest to discuss them only when the issue is properly before the people. I would point out that many of the splendid Englishmen, Scotchmen and Irishmen who came to Canada were single men, whose relatives were not with them. They were living on homesteads in the Northwest, working on the railways, in the mines and forests, as labouring men or farmers; as mechanics in the cities and towns. They had no incumbrances, and the moment the call to arms came, they were ready to jump into harness. Our boys on the farms had to think about it. They did come on in splendid numbers, though; the regiment commanded by Colonel Watson of Quebec, which comes from the eastern part of the province of Ontario, was made up entirely of boys from the farms of Ontario; so with other Ontario
regiments. Here is another phase of the matter:	read the Canadian casualty lists
and you will be amazed when you observe how many United States-born volunteers are fighting with the Canadian troops. A couple of dozen of persons from the United States have already fallen at the front. There are hundreds of Americans in the service, fighting not for the adventure, but for the principle of liberty. From the outset I have recognized, publicly and privately, that our French Canadian fellow countrymen have done splendid service. We are organizing another French Canadian regiment; another could be filled inside of a week and fill another one immediately afterwards, if it were required. They are doing their duty splendidly.
Allowances, active militia, $130,000.

Since the outbreak of the war there have been several promotions of officers in the inside service of the Department of Militia. I am free to admit that the officers of the Militia Department have had thrust upon them a great responsibility and an immense amount of work. I feel that I can speak for every member of the House in saying that the honours thus conferred on the officers of the Militia Department have been worthily conferred and I would like to offer my congratulations to the officers of the department, beginning with the minister himself and including the deputy minister, on the promotions that have come to them. No matter how we may differ as to the manner in which some of that work devolving on the officers of the department has been performed, the work has been of a most arduous character; and I can readily understand that they have been at a great nervous tension for a good many months. I think the honours which have been conferred have been worthily bestowed.

On behalf of
the officers I thank the hon. member for what he has said. Referring to the item before us, the allowances are for command pay, drill instruction, postage, and trumpeters' and signallers' gratuities on qualifying. A great many extra trumpeters and signallers have qualified and they receive a small gratuity on doing so.

The minister referred to members of the active militia qualifying. Would he tell me whether, if an officer goes to Kingston or Halifax and takes a qualifying course, that is charged up to the ordin-

ary revenue account or the special war vote? From the returns it would appear that almost everything in regard to the militia has been charged to the war vote.
The expenses of officers for the militia are charged to the training vote, and for overseas to the war vote.
Does it not appear to my hon. friend that he might reduce the $130,000?
These are for the militia officers all over the country.
One would think that practically all the militia training now would be with a view to overseas service. I understood from the minister that these expenses are defrayed out of the war vote.

Oh, no. I have the details by divisions for command pay, drill instruction, etc. For that alone there was a considerable increase. The new corps that have been established involve quite an addition to the expense.

Are non-coms, and men of the ordinary active militia being trained except with a view to overseas service? For instance, take the expense for drill instruction. The annual drill has been abolished, and I think rightly, and I congratulate the minister on dropping that $2,000,000 of expenditure. Why is it necessary, then, to keep paying out money for drill instruction?
This is for command pay and drill instruction. We must keep these officers, they receive so much each year for care of arms and drill instruction.
My own old corps, the 10th field battery, has no officers; there is no battery and there are no arms.
I understand they are training officers for that very battery, and that applications have come in.
I did not know that, but I know that the battery has gone to the front.

Every corps that has been depleted for the front is being filled up again as rapidly as possible, and some of them have been filled two or three times over. Corps with a strength of 700 or 800 have already sent to the front twice as many men as their regular establishments.
That course has not been carrid out in regard to my own old corps, the 10th Field Battery.

This is the first opportunity we have had of discussing militia matters in general, because we have had no discussion when the Speaker was in the Chair, as we on this side of the House have not, insisted upon our rights, but have been quite willing to take up the Estimates whenever the ministers were ready. Might it be understood that on some of these items we might discuss all military matters if we desired to do so?
As far as I am concerned that could be done.
What arrangements has the minister made as to the appointment of censors throughout Canada?

Wherever
there is a cable or Marconi station we have censors, and we have some at headquarters here.
What are the average salaries paid them and how many are there?

There are 13 censors, 40 assistant censors and 78 decoders. There is a cable station and a Marconi station with officers receiving cablegrams. The deputy chief censor receives S10 a day; the censors, $9; the as-sitant censors, $7; and the decoders, $3.50.
Is $10 a day paid to the chief censors all over the country ?
There is only one-Lieutenant # Colonel Hamilton.
Is he obliged to give all his time to the duties which he performs for the Government ?
Night and day; his office is open all the time.
It is rumoured that he has been engaged in writing party pamphlets for the Conservative party since he has been appointed.
I am in the fortunate position of having never seen a party sheet, either of the boozorium literature or the Tory literature.

My hon. friend is wise in not paying attention to verbal or newspaper criticism, because if he did he would find that the criticism of him has not been greater on the Liberal side than on

the Conservative side. My hon. friend is wise in not paying much attention to the grumblings and complaints that are made in regard to his actions in the discharge of his important duties. Are there censors at St. John?
Wherever there *is a MaTconi station there are censors. I understand that there are three at St. John.

The other evening my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who is usuahy very intelligent and. very well informed, was putting his Estimates through and I made inquiries as to the censors at St. John. The minister was unable to tell me anything about them, but he said that the Minister of Militia would be able to give me that information. So now, I avail myself of the opportunity of asking the Minister of Militia how many censors there are at St. John, what salaries they are receiving and what their duties are.
I received the information from my hon. friend the Minister of the Naval Service, who has been kind enough to tell me that there are three.	-
What are their salaries?

There are
three censors at Partridge, island, and they receive $7 a day. I do not know their names.

I am told that their names are: Mr. Shaw, who is a young lawyer and a very deserving gentleman, Mr. Masters an insurance agent, also a deserving gentleman, and Mr. Crockett. I do not know his occupation, except it is that of a party friend and worker.

Are they
Tories ? As a rule they are Liberals.

I do not know, I am sure, as to that. My hon. friend can guess as to their political complexion when he knows that they were recommended by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He would not be so forgetful about the claims of party friends as to recommend gentlemen on our side. I do not blame him for that. What are the duties of these censors and how many despatches go through the wireless station at Partridge island in the course of a day ? The feeling of a great many people is that three censors at Partridge island are entirely unnecessary. The statement made to me is that each of these
censors performs his duty about two days in the week and rests from his arduous labours during the remaining five days.

I will be
only too glad to get the information as to the duties of these gentlemen. They revise all the despatches that go through. Anything of an improper character will be stopped. They have to send a copy of every one of these despatches to the chief censor daily for criticism. They are supposed to give all their time to their duties. I will make inquiries.
I would like to find out how much has been paid to each of these gentlemen from the time of his appointment to the present and the number of despatches censored weekly.
We will find that out.
It may be that my information is entirely unfounded. It may be that these gentlemen are earning, by the power of tlfeir intellects, not by the sweat of their brows, the salaries that they re" ceive.

I had a question on the Order Paper the other day winch the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) refused to answer on the ground that the information was confidential. The question had reference to the anchoring of the fleet in uaspS bay. I wanted to make the best showing I could for Gaspe bay; it is a magnificent sheet of water, and I wanted to bring out its good points. I asked certain information about the number of boats that were anchored there while transporting the Canadian contingent, but I was unable to get a reply. However, I have received from Salisbury a post-card giving tne names of all these boats, tha depth of water at the anchorage and so on. The information is entirely public. The Prime Minister said that these matters were confident.al and that he did not like to answer my question. I want to call the minister's attention to the fact that tne Montreal Star, the aay after the contingent arrived in England, published a page or two containing much more information than I asked for in my question. I do not know whetuer tne Star did this under censorship -r whether the censorship as to Canadian newspapers was in force.

There were
one or two parts of the question asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) that did not deal merely with tnese matters of anchorage

the best showing I could for Gaspe bay; and the like of that and which it was tnought we** not to answer. As far as Gaspe basin is concerned, every one knows wnat it is; -he charts show it. But I did not think it desirable to answer the other questions that t**e hon. gentl man asked.
Mr. MARCH,:	Was it the censorship
that was exercised over the Canadian papers which enabled them to publish this information only after the contingent had reached England?

The papers
have been very good. It was not deemed advisable that any reference should be made to the sailing of the Canadian contingent and the Canadian papers have been very loyal in observing the requests of the censors in this respect. It was requested that they should publish nothing about the sailing of the contingent until after they had arrived in England. The daily papers have done splendid service.
Is the censorship still in existence?

Yes. I had
the privilege for the first time of seeing Gaspe basin when the boys went away, and I entirely agree with everytning the hon. gentleman has said. It is one of the most magnificent sheets of water that it has ever been my privilege to see.

Will the pensions be paid according to the rank which the man held in the militia of Canada, or according to the rank in which he is serving in the war? There are many officers in the Canadian militia who are serving as privates in our overseas force; will they be pensioned according to their rank here or their rank on active service?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the absence of any special provision, 1 think the regulation would be construed as meaning the rank which they held while in active service.
Here?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, at the front. Suppose a mail holding the rank of captain or lieutenant in the Canadian militia, finding it impossible to get a commission should go to the front as a private, I should think under the construction of these regulations as they are framed at present although they are not yet passed, the pension would have to be determined by the rank held at the front. The pension regu-

lations have not yet been passed, and I jyould be perfectly willing to consider any suggestion with regard to that matter. I did not ask that the pension resolutions should be considered to-day, as I thought it would be desirable to have suggestions from hon. members before we finally decided on their form.

As the resolutions are at present drawn, I should think that a man who. enlisted as a private, no matter what his rank in the Canadian militia, and who served as a private at the front, would only get the pension allowed to a private. I was asked the question by one of the men to-day, and my impression was the same as that of the Prime Minister. Whether or not it would be proper to change that I do not know.

If a Canadian serving in the militia of Canada is a captain in good standing, and has rendered good service to the country, and not being able to get a commission to go to the front, his patriotism impels him to go as a private, I think the country should recognize the position he held in the Canadian militia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Something might be said on the other side, but I will not argue the other side for the moment. I shall be glad to consider it. We have examples of a great many men of high commissioned rank in the Canadian militia, who have gone to the front in very subordinate positions, rather than not have an opportunity to serve. Examples of that character are not confined to this country, because I understand there are two rear-admirals in Great Britain who, having no opportunity for active service in their rank, accepted service as commanders and as juniors to about 250 commanders, who previously had served in a rank far below them. It occurs to me that it would be rather difficult, indeed almost impracticable, to work out any arrangement as to pensions other .than that which I have mentioned. But my mind is open upon the subject. My hon. friend and colleague, the Minister of Militia, has had his time so much taken up with other matters that I have been obliged to give my personal attention to the question of pensions, and I have had it more under consideration than he.

A good many officers accepted service as privates, but that practice we have stopped. Realizing that a number of' splendid men have ac-

cepted active service in a rank much below their rank in the militia of Canada, we have in every case guaranteed these men their rank and their status when they return from the war.
Why are officers not now permitted to enlist as privates?

The law is
that before an officer can enlist as a private he has to resign his commission, and it was upsetting the internal economy of the force to have a man regarded as a private in one place and as a captain in another. In any event we thought we could utilize these men as officers, and we are watching that pretty carefully.
What is the Minister of Militia paying for automatic pistols, 45 calibre?
I think it is $18.50.
I wish to call attention to the fact that on the -22nd of September an order in council was passed on the recommendation of the acting minister- who was acting minister at that time?
I really don't know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may have been the guilty party, but I am not sure.

On the 22nd of Sephyn-ber an order in council was passed on the recommendation of the acting minister, giving authority to purchase for the Canadian military forces 1,000 automatic pistols at a price not exceeding $18.50. What does the minister pay for ammunition for these automatic pistols?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I know what my hon. friend alludes to. A report came in from the deputy minister with regard to the purchase of ammunition which contained a clerical mistake, which was rectified as soon as discovered. I signed the report to council upon the recommendation of the deputy minister, not knowing the particulars, and the next day or the day after, the deputy minister discovered that there was a clerical error in the price fixed for th^ ammunition, and it was corrected in a subsequent order in council.
The correction appears to have been made on the recommendation of the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I presume the minister had returned in the meantime.
It should have been $18.50 instead of $40.00?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
That explanation is satisfactory. As I understand it, .303, mark vii, small-arms ammunition, is the favourite ammunition.

It is the
latest.
How many millions of rounds of that ammunition are now under order by the department, being manufactured for the Canadian Government?

20,000,000
rounds-5,000,000 and 15,000,000 from the Dominion Cartridge Company. There is also an order for 10,000,000 from an American firm.
What are the prices charged by the Remington?
$34 on some orders and $35 on others.
And by the Dominion Cartridge Company?
What was the price early last fall?

Last fall, in
August or September, I was negotiating for some ammunition for the Imperial authorities. The price asked by one concern in the United States was $42.50 per thousand, and by another concern in the United States $37.50. That was the lowest price obtainable at that time. An offer was then obtained for 75,000,000 rounds at $33, the lowest price at which ammunition has been obtained from the beginning of the war. I understand that $47.50 has been paid.
Who gave that order?

The British
Government.
Through whom?
The Minister of Militia for the Dominion of Canada.
Was it given by my hon. friend personally or through another party?
It was given by the Minister of Militia personally.
Verbally or in writing?
There was a regular signed contract.
Would my hon. friend bring down the correspondence with reference to it?

No, I will not. It does not concern the Canadian Government. I am following the custom of my good friends opposite at the time of the South African war. Anything of that kind will have to be obtained from the Imperial authorities. I shall be only too delighted to forward any request that my hon. friend may make. The matter, however, concerns the British authorities.
My hon. friend was good enough to tell me there was a written contract made through my hon. friend?
I was the agent.
When was that contract made?
In the latter part of August or early in September.

Was that contract
negotiated in New York by Mr. J. Wesley Allison and associates?

I have no hesitation in saying that Mr. J. Wesley Allison was the gentleman through whom the reduction from $42.50 to $37.50 was negotiated, and then from $37.50 to $33. The country owes him a large debt of gratitude.
Who appointed him?
I did.
Has my hon. friend any correspondence with Mr. J. Wesley Allison which he will bring down?
I have nothing which should be or which need be brought down. There is nothing to be brought down.
There was no correspondence with Mr. J. Wesley Allison?
No.

Will the minister give the names of the firms from which those
75,000,000 rounds of ammunition were purchased?.
The Remington Arms Union Metallic Company of the United States.
Only one company?
One company. I do not know where they got the ammunition.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that there appears in these memoranda, on page 38, a copy of an Order in Council of the 4th September, 1914, as follows:
The committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Militia and ' Defence, advise that a contract be made with the Dominion Cartridge Company, Limited, of Montreal, for the manufacture of 5,000,000 rounds of .303, mark vii, small arms ammunition, at $31 per thousand rounds.
Does my hon. friend say that at the time when the order was given to the Dominion Cartridge Company for 5,000,000 rounds of small arms ammunition at $31 per thousand rounds, the price in the United States was the price which my hon. friend has stated, namely, $42.50?

This $31 was for
5.000.	000 rounds from the Dominion Cartridge Company. It was a couple of weeks subsequent to that date that the American prices were obtained. This bargain, although the Order in Council was passed on September 4, 1914, was entered into many weeks before that date. The company have already made the ammunition.

The first order was for
5.000.	000 rounds at $31 per thousand. When was the next order given in Canada to the same company?
The next order was given in my absence, possibly in the month of October.

At page 41 of the memoranda, I find an order of the 17th of October,, given to the Remington Arms Union Metallic Company, of Bridgeport, United States, at $33 per thousand, for the Canadian Government. Was that the next order given?
That is the American order. There was another order for 15,000,000 rounds at $35.
Which company?
The Dominion Cartridge Company.	*

What page on the
memoranda.

That order
was subsequent to the printing of the memoranda.

What was the date of
that order?
We will ascertain the date for the hon. member.
What compensation was given to Mr. J. Wesley Allison for his services?
Nothing whatever. Mr. Allison declined any remuneration so far as anything connected with the Dominion of Canada was concerned. The case is different so far as Russia or Great Britain is concerned.

My hon. friend said that Mr. Allison was acting for the Imperial Government on the appointment of the Minister of Militia, and that he made this contract on behalf of the Minister of Militia and on behalf of the Imperial Government for
75,000,000 rounds at $33 per thousand. Does my hon. friend know the place at which the contract between Mr. Allison and the Remington Arms Company was entered into?
I entered into the contract myself. Does the hon. gentleman wish to know the exact spot?
It is not very material.

It is a little
station called Moira in the Adirondack mountains. The contract was entered into at seven o'clock. I had not had my dinner then. Does my hon. friend wish to know any other details about the matter?
Mr. PUGSLE1T:	My hon. friend made
the agreement with the Remington Arms Company which resulted in the signing of the contract?
Mr. Allison has been instrumental in bringing the prices down.

I did not ask my hon.
friend for that.
Mr. Allison did not make the contract; I made the contract, and it was entered into at that spot.
My hon. friend said that the negotiations were carried on by Mr. Allison. I would ask the minister whether or not Mr. Allison carried on the negotiations in New York?
New York State?
I mean the city of New York. But perhaps the minister knows nothing about that.

I do not know.
It is a matter of no importance-New York or anywhere else.	,

I will tell the hon. minister what I have been informed; and he will be able to set the rumours at rest if they are not true. I have been informed that previous to Mr. Allison appearing on the scene representing the Canadian Government and the British Government in the purchase of ammunition, the manufacturers of this class of ammunition had practically fixed the price at $36.50 per 1,000 rounds; that Mr. Allison entered into correspondence in New York with the manufacturers, with the result that the manufacturers broke their contracts with the gentleman who was about to purchase for the British Government, and the price was reduced to $33 per 1,000 rounds.

Would the
hon. gentleman have any objection to stating the name of his informant. If he gives the information, he ought to be willing to give the name of the one from whom he got the information.

If the minister will
promise to investigate the matter, I will give the name of my informant. He will find on record the proceedings now pending in one of the courts of New York in which the question is raised as to these manufacturers having broke their contract with the gentleman who was about buying for the British Government. I will give what information I have, because I am sure the hon. gentleman will not willingly be a party to anything like that. That is the statement-that Mr. Allison with the gentlemen associated with him went to New York, took apartments at the Manhattan Hotel, and put himself forward as the representative of the Canadian Government and the British Government and ready to negotiate-
I am in a position to state that there is not a word of truth directly or indirectly in what is stated by the hon. gentleman. If he will permit me, I will tell him the facts.
I shall be glad.
He is up the wrong tree.	-
Which is the right tree?

The lawsuit
to which the hon. gentleman refers does not concern this affair at all. It has to do with a Yankee concern called Flint & Co., that is claiming something on ammunition, ordered for the British Government, with which Major Allison and the Canadian Government had nothing to do. I do not know the details-do not want to know them. But I understand they are entering 11 p.m. an action against the Remington Company, claiming a commission on twenty or forty million rounds of mark vi ammunition ordered by the British Government. I would nbt, as representative of the British Government, be found guilty of ordering mark VI ammuni tion. It is obsolete. And as to the price, I do not know-
It was $26.50.

If that is the price for mark vi ammunition, all I have to say is that it is very high. Mark vii was ordered in advance of the war, and the price of it was $31 at that time. At the time the negotiations were carried on through Mr. Allison for me, and when the contract was arranged with the British Government-the hon. gentleman is not entitled to get this information, but I am giving it to him.

It is very good of the
minister to give it.

Very good.
The price was $42.50 by one concern, and $37.50 by Flint & Co., which was the lowest we could get it; but it was arranged at $33, which,is $4.50 less than the lowest price ammunition lias been purchased for in America.
That was accomplishing a great deal for the British Government. Can the minister tell me how he came to employ Mr. Allison to make these negotiations?

He has been for thirty-five years my personal friend, and he is a gentlemen in whom I have every confidence. He is absolutely well-posted, and I have found him the soul of honour. He is also most patriotic. At a time when certain gentlemen were negotiating for the transfer of a water-power on the St. Lawrence to an American organization on terms under which ninety-five per cent of the power would have been used in the United States and five per cent in Canada, [Mr. Pugsley.l
Mr. Allison carried on at his own expense- with your humble servant-the opposition to this scheme much to the discomfiture of these gentlemen.
Did Mr. Allison formerly have an office in New York?
I do not know.
Is this the J. Wesley Allison who had a celebrated patent shovel, and who had material brought over in the night from Waddington?

He is the man who, at the outbreak of the war, learning that the British Government was getting large supplies from the United States of America, made arrangements that neither the British nor the Canadian Government could improve upon; had the materials shipped in, in daylight-he is not a man who operates in the dark or behind the scenes; had it brought in bond to Canada and sent across to the British Government; and later instructed the authorities that the material could be shipped direct from New York without the circumlocution .-of going through Canada. Does the hon. gentleman want any further information?

Yes, on botn shovels and ammunition. Will the minister tell me what quantity of ammunition, described as .303, mark vii, small-arms ammunition, was purchased in the United 'States by Mr. Allison for the Canadian Government?
He did not purchase for the Canadian Government.
Who made that purchase?

I was in
Europe at the time.
I speak of the ammunition purchased pursuant to the Order in Council of the I7th October, 1914.
It was the same arrangement, I am informed, as I carried on for the British Government.

I thank the minister for the information he has given. Perhaps he will give me more by bringing down the correspondence in regard to the purchase of ten million rounds pursuant to the Order in Council of the 17th October, 1914.
Yes, I have nothing to hide.

I am not suggesting that there is anything to hide. But the minis-

'ter must see that it looks strange that a middleman should be employed to secure this ten million rounds. It may he capable of explanation, hut he will he given the opportunity.
After the hon. gentleman has been insinuating-
When?
I am told that he made the statement that this ammunition could have been had at $26 instead of at $33. That is erroneous.
That is my information.
It is absolutely wrong; and I can tell the hon. gentleman that there was no middleman in the case. Mr. Allison is not a middleman.
Not a middleman?

He was not a middleman. He is my friend, just as Mr. Ellis is my friend, who engaged in purchasing field-glasses, and whom I trusted to carry on this work and obtain these goods for the British Government and break down the grafting rings that were seeking to rob both Canada and Great Britain, and to get these goods at a fairly representative price.
Is Mr. Powell included in that category?
Mr. Powell is not employed by the Minister of Militia.
Do I understand that the minister draws a distinction between middlemen; that Mr. Allison was not a middleman because he was a personal friend of the minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is misrepresenting the Minister of Militia; I hope he is not doing so purposely. The Minister of Militia has explained that a contract for 75,000,000 rounds of ammunition was made personally by him at the request of the British Government. Before he entered into that contract he asked Mr. Allison to obtain, and Mr. Allison did obtain, information for him as to the price at which it could be secured, and as to the sources from which it might be obtained. The contract was made by the minister; Mr. Allison had no interest in the contract by way of commission or otherwise, and received no remuneration for his services.

The hon.
gentleman will readily understand that
there were any number of agents here from the United States, and the lowest price which could be obtained in respect of this . ammunition was $42.50 per thousand rounds. I knew that the price was outrageous, and I refused to order. The two firms with which negotiations were had were Peters, of Cincinnati, and Flint & Co., of New York. Flint & Co. finally came down to $37.50. I knew that that was still too high, so I sent for Mr. Allison, knowing that he knew these gentlemen and knowing that I could trust him. In less than a week Mr. Allison had negotiated the price down to $33.
My hon. friend will agree that the enormous quantity of 75,000,000 rounds was the biggest order given for many years, if not the biggest order ever placed with this firm.

An order for
300.000.	000 rounds had been given a short time before that by the British Government.
To the same firm?
No, to other firms, and they paid far more for it.
Will my hon. friend bring down the correspondence with regard to the 10,000,000 rounds ?

As to our
10.000.	000, certainly.

Mr. Chairman, some time ago I asked a question which reads as follows:-
Who had been appointed to purchase in the province of Quebec from the 1st of July to the 1st of December, 1914, the horses required for the militia, or for the first contingent?
In reply it was stated that the chief veterinary surgeon and his assistants had been purchasing these horses. I would like to know the names of this chief veterinary surgeon and of his assistants in the province of Quebec.
The veterinary for the province of Quebec was Colonel Piche.
Had instructions been given this Mr. Piche to purchase horses in certain specified parts of the province of Quebec, or did he have a free hand in making those purchases?

Arrangements have been made whereby every part of the province of Quebec will be visited. It was reported that the district of which my

hon. friend speaks did not produce good artillery horses, but it has been found that horses quite suitable for artillery purposes may be obtained from my hon. friend's province.
I saw a corps parading the streets of Ottawa the other day; thousands of horses just as good could be obtained in the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe.
That has not been generally known, but the buyers have been informed. They are good horses, well fitted for all kinds of rough climatic conditions.
What proportion of the regular militia have volunteered for active service ?

I have not the exact figures before me. Judging by the returns, in many localities whole corps have volunteered. Of course, every regiment contains a certain number of men who have families; others we will not part with because we require them at home for instruction purposes. The response of the active militia has been simply magnificent.
In some localities that has not been the case.
Probably due to local causes. '

It is said that in some places the active militia did not respond in this crisis as they should have done, arid that a much larger proportion of persons who were not members of the militia responded to the call.

I did know one case in respect of which it was that that charge could be made, but on inquiry it was found that the eolonel and senior major had gone to the front, the junior major was absent for some reason, and the next in command was not as aggressive an officer as he might have been. We placed the next senior captain in command, and since that time the regiment has turned out much better.
Is it the intention of the Government to bring into Ottawa volunteers who are assembled in small centres like Alexandria, Brockville and Smith's Falls?

During the winter months the men have been mobilized at the various localities. We have no place

to drill them during the winter season, but With the coming of spring and the disappearing of the snow, they will be mobilized in the larger centres. The snow in the West has disappeared, but not in the East, and the camps are not fit for occupation. It is our intention, however, to take them into the camps where they will get rifle shooting and all the advantages of manoeuvring.

An article appeared in the Ottawa Free Press of Marchl7, headed: " Little Towns Want to Keep the Soldiers; Politicians are Delaying Mobilization of Contingent." Further down it says:
The men at these different centres received, besides their pay, sustenance allowance of 75 cents a day.
In the case of Alexandria this means more than $500 a week to be spent on board and lodging. Brockville is slightly under this while Smiths Falls benefits to a considerably larger extent. The soldiers who always know where the next pay is coming from spend quite freely. At present they have little work to do and have lots of time to get out and squander their money. Certainly politicians who see the advantage of this to the towns and likewise the Government, are anxious to have the condition continue as long as possible.
Speaking for Alexandria and the soldiers there now, I do not suppose that the soldiers training in Ottawa give one-half the time to their work that soldiers training in Alexandria do at the present time. We have a gentleman there who spent 21 years in the British army and I question if there is in Ottawa his equal in the drilling and training of men. We are out in the country and in our county we have not a single hotel license, so we are perfectly dry. When you talk about the men getting out and squandering their money, I do not know how they are to squander it.
Ice cream?

Ice cream and champagne cider I suppose. I think in fairness that the Militia Department should hesitate about calling these men in. Until the season comes when you can concentrate them at some larger camp they can do quite as well if not better in the small towns. We have quite as good discipline and the outside attractions are not many. I think it would be too bad to take away from the small towns the little advantage they may gain by having soldiers centered there, we think mat we are entitled to some consideration. Ottawa is not entitled to every-tning. li ceriainly has its share of soldiers and I would ask the minister, before

recalling the men from Alexandria, to look into the matter very closely.	.

We have
given it a greau deal of study and the people have been assisting us to do so; the officers have been demanaing that the men be mobilized and the localities nave been demanding that they-be kept there, the object being the monetary advantage which my hon. friend has reierred to. At the local centres the men cannot be finally passed medically or finally uniformed and equipped or properly organized. The officers who are now over them will not be over them in the regiment when it is formed. It would take two or three weeks to do that. We have held them back in these localities all winter and I am pleased to say that Alexandria is one of the finest portions of the Dominion of Canada. There is a splendid drill hall there which my hon. friend was instrumental in having built, and he has given every assistance to the cause in his locality. We have received complaints that we have kept the men in these localities a week or two weeks too long. Areas are now open in the larger centres for drilling and the officers want to get the men' in uniform and test them, which takes a week or two. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that our object is to get the men ready for service, not to benefit localities. We have tried to play the game both ways, to keep them in the localities during the winter; but now that spring is coming on we are bringing them to the mobilizing centres and organizing them to get them into shape for the camp as soon as the weather opens up, in two or three weeks time.

Will the minister have
another Valcartier?

In the case of the first contingent there was a rush. The second contingent, without mentioning any Rate, will probably go before the St. Lawrence route or Valcartier will be ready. This will not be till about the middle of May, so that it would be impossible to concentrate the camp for the second contingent there.

Is the editor of
. the Toronto Telegram an officer?
I am not sure.
He is very much in favour of having the drill take place in the smaller places.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: His views are different from mine.

I am sorry to disagree
with my hon. friend from Glengarry (Mr. McMillan) but I am assuming that the minister is looking at this thing entirely from the standpoint of the militia and not from that of the local merchants and local aspirations. I have heard a great many complaints from different members of the army because they have been kept at local headquarters and not placed in a central camp. I speak from my own experience, because years ago I was a member of the militia for a great many years, and I always found that the training we got at local headquarters, while useful, was not of great service when we were brigaded with other forces at large camps. A great deal has been said about Valcartier, and there is no doubt there were many mistakes made in the equipment of that camp, but for all that I am very strongly of the opinion that the larger the camp of training that the minister can organize the better for the soldiers, and after all that is the important thing.
I know that many officers have complained to me during the past two or three months that they are getting tired of remaining in local headquarters and the men are demanding a change. I am very much of the opinion that the minister will do well to get them together in as large bodies as possible, and it does seem to me that he could not do better than go to Valcartier. There must be enough units under arms to-day in Canada to tax the capacity of a place like Valcartier. I am sure that the minister'will find the consensus of opinion of the militia themselves and the officers is that they should be got together in as large camps as possible.

I agree with what my hon. friend says. Two weeks ago I had men visit Valcartier and they found three feet of snow on the ground there then. There are two and a half feet there now, and there is no chance that that snow will disappear in time for the camp. Otherwise I think my friend will have no fault to find with my plans.
I might tell the Minister of Militia that there is no snow at Petawawa. -
Will my hon. friend tell us where Petawawa is?

2,500. I may say that the women have been the best recruiting officers we have. The splendid spirit displayed by the women of Canada has been a credit to Canada.
How many have been accepted?

All the British Government asked for. We do not send them of our own accord, only the number they ask for.
Mr. .MARCIL: Is the minister not sending any nurses with the regiments going this summer?

We do not send them as regiments but as hospitals. It depends on the nature of the hospital, whether it is a base or a stationery or a field hospital, whether we send nurses with it or not.
